CH01.text:
[CH01 | 0:00–0:36 | 沉浸式开场：第一秒落地时空身位，挂出两条任务线，建立第一人称在场框架]

This is a stone altar. It was supposed to have four carved sides showing the king's glory. It has one. The chisels are still sitting there. No one has touched them in two years.

I'm a Maya priest in 822 AD—ah k'in, the one who keeps the calendar, marks the ceremonies, watches the monuments. This is Copán, and I walk past this thing every single day.

Here's what I know: the king ordered this altar carved two years ago. One side finished—the king's coronation scene, perfect detail. The second side? Started and stopped. Two sides completely blank. And those chisels. Still right there. Waiting for hands that never came back.

This isn't just a delayed project. When your job is to maintain eternity—to mark time, to promise the gods that tomorrow will come like today came—a stone that stops being carved is a different kind of record. It's a record of stopping.

I need to go to the palace and find out why. I need to understand what happened to the carvers, what happened to the plan. And I need to tell the king something he probably already knows but won't admit: something has changed.

CH02.text:
[CH02 | 0:36–1:12 | 真实性契约与制作说明：声明素材来源、复原方法、时代标注，建立观众对'所见即所考'的信任]

Before we go further, you need to know where this comes from.

Everything you're seeing is reconstructed from real artifacts. Stone reliefs from Copán and other southern lowland cities. Murals painted on temple walls. Pottery decorated with ritual scenes. All of it exists in museums and archaeological records, in the public domain.

The method is straightforward: I take the original relief carvings—the outlines, the figures, the glyphs—and use AI to add color and build the environments around them, as close to the archaeological evidence as we can get.

One complication: some of the ritual details come from a Spanish friar named Diego de Landa, who documented Yucatan Maya ceremonies in the 1560s. That's 600 years after the Classic period collapse. But the basic structure of priest roles and ritual practices seems to have carried through. I'll tell you when we're bridging that gap.

So what does a priest actually do every day? What are the tasks that can stop?

CH03.text:
[CH03 | 1:12–1:48 | 任务简报与探索清单：列出祭司的两条行动线，同时暗示中点的两个对比性结局]

As town priest—ah k'in—you announce feast days, conduct rituals, oversee monument carving.

You've been noticing things. Carvers: no lime, trees gone. Ceremony crowds: half. The rains? Didn't come.

Two tasks: see the palace zones. Find the king, tell him.

Will they listen? And how do you get in?

CH04.text:
[CH04 | 1:48–3:08 | 进入神庙区的阶层检查与日常生活流：用感官细节与现代参照系建立'活人感'，同时展示权力等级制度]

First: your daily work. You walk into the temple precinct. Copal incense—thick, sweet, almost sticky in your throat. There's your desk: stone carved with calendar wheels, two circles that never quite line up. Tree-bark paper stacked on one side. Red ink, black ink. Today you'll copy tribute lists, check the feast day schedule.

Two calendars run at once. The 260-day Tzolk'in—sacred calendar, for divination, for naming children, for knowing which god holds power today. The 365-day Haab'—solar calendar, eighteen months of twenty days, plus five unlucky days at year's end. They mesh like gears. Every 52 years they click back to the same starting point. That's one Calendar Round. Most people live one, maybe see the start of a second.

This system is ten times more complex than a lunar calendar. You spent your childhood learning to track both wheels, predict their meetings, never let them slip. That's your job: keep the wheels turning.

But here's the thing. The high priest—ahau can mai—he walks straight into the palace. No announcement, no waiting. You? You send word through an attendant. You wait for permission. Same knowledge, different doors. That's how power looks in space.

Today you have ritual work: preparing for the year-bearer ceremony. They'll need you to confirm the date, arrange the offerings.

Your job is to make sure these wheels don't fail. Except they're already failing. And no one with direct access seems to notice.

So: the palace. What does it look like when you finally get in?

CH05.text:
[CH05 | 3:08–4:20 | 与同事/助手的对话与仪式供品清单：用配角的小梦想人化遇难者，预告当晚活动，同时暗示资源消耗]

The copal smoke is thick today. Your assistant, Chac, is sorting the bundles on the preparation table—dried corn husks, bound in twine the way they always are. He's humming something, moving his hands with the kind of casual rhythm that comes from doing this a thousand times.

"I was thinking," he says, not looking up. "After I finish helping with the ceremonies this season, maybe I ask for my own posting. A town priest in one of the smaller settlements. My son is learning the glyphs. If I move up, he learns faster. Better teacher, better lineage."

He says it like he's already decided. Like the path is already there.

You hand him the tree bark paper—the white sheets they'll need to catch the blood tonight. Years ago, this stack would be twice as thick. You don't mention it.

"The offerings are ready," he continues, still organizing. "Copal. Corn. Two chickens for the year-bearer ceremony." He taps the bundle. "That should be enough."

Should be. Last month, the high priest's ceremony had twice the copal. The month before that, more. Now it's been cut quietly, no announcement. The supplies get smaller and nobody says why. Chac's eyes have started noticing what his mouth won't say out loud.

You watch him check the inventory. Copal resin in its clay bowl. Corn in its basket. The tree bark paper stacked and ready. The tools for the bloodletting arranged in precise order—the stingray spine, the obsidian blade, the bowl to catch what flows.

"We should move soon," you say. "Change into the ceremonial garments. The ceremony starts before the sun reaches its peak."

Chac nods, rolling the last bundle carefully. He looks at you for a moment—really looks at you, like he wants to ask something but doesn't. Then he glances back at his work.

"Will you come see the new stela I carved? After everything?" He's carved one for the palace courtyard, his first major work. It has the king's face, the date glyph, the usual forms. "It's nothing like what the master stoneworkers did twenty years ago, but... it's what I could manage with what we have."

You promise you will. You both know what that means—if there's anything left to see.

CH06.text:
[CH06 | 4:20–5:34 | 集体仪式高光与小型社群时刻：用归属感与共同体验制造情绪高峰，为后段的崩解蓄能]

That night, there's a ceremony in the plaza—one of the year-bearer rituals. The city gathers.

Torches line the perimeter. Drums echo off the pyramid steps. Copal smoke fills the air, thick and sweet, pressing down like the humidity before rain. You can feel the heat of bodies packed close, hundreds of people swaying in rhythm.

The nobles go first. They use stingray spines and obsidian blades—piercing their tongues, letting the blood drip onto bark paper strips laid at their feet. Some of the royal blood relatives do it publicly, right here on the plaza platform. The paper soaks through dark red, then gets rolled and burned in the braziers.

Then the commoners. Most pierce their earlobes—quick, small offerings. A few do their tongues if they're asking for something specific. Everyone bleeds. Everyone participates.

And in that moment, standing in the smoke and the drumbeat, you hear someone say it out loud: "This is our promise to the gods. We bleed, they send rain."

The whole plaza believes it. You can see it in their faces—the certainty, the shared commitment. This is what holds everything together. This contract.

When the ceremony ends and people start to drift away, one of the senior priests—someone you've worked with for years—catches your eye. Doesn't say anything. Just tilts his head slightly toward the edge of the plaza, away from the torches.

You follow him into the shadows between two residential compounds. He waits until the drumming fades and the plaza empties before he speaks.

CH07.text:
[CH07 | 5:34–6:56 | 内部知情者的坦白与危机确认：用私密对话完成'元设定溶解'，锁定观众对危机迹象的第一次完整认知]

"The stone carvers," he says. Voice low. "They told you about the trees?"

You nod.

"They told me the same thing three months ago. No trees left close enough to haul. Can't burn lime without fuel. That altar—" He doesn't finish. Doesn't need to.

"It's not just the trees," you say. "Last month's ceremony. The Year Bearer procession. I counted maybe forty people in the plaza. Maybe. A year ago there were hundreds."

He doesn't look surprised. Just tired.

"The rains," he says. It's not a question. "The king promised. We performed the bloodletting. We gave the offering. The year turned over. The rains didn't come."

You both stand there. Not speaking. The contract is supposed to work. The king bleeds, the gods send rain, the maize grows. That's the deal. That's how time continues.

"Tomorrow," he says finally. "The king is holding a private ceremony at dawn. In the palace compound. If you're going to say something—if anyone's going to say something—that's the window."

He meets your eyes. Waits. Then nods once and walks back toward the plaza.

You stand in the dark a little longer. Everything just changed. You're not the only one who sees it anymore. But knowing together doesn't make it lighter. It makes it heavier.

You go back to your quarters. Tomorrow you'll go to the palace. But tonight—tonight you just stand there, looking at the empty plaza, wondering: if we all see it, why are we still pretending the ceremonies will hold? Why can't we just tell the king what's breaking?

CH08.text:
[CH08 | 6:56–8:00 | 进入王宫礼仪区的禁入奇观：用阶层对比与材质细节制造视觉冲击，同时加深任务的紧迫感]

You find a reason to enter the palace ceremonial zone—assisting with tomorrow's ritual preparations. The moment you step through, everything changes.

Jade inlay catches the torchlight. Painted stucco—reds, blues, whites—covers every surface in patterns you've never seen this dense. The courtyard opens up three times the width of the plaza you work in. Light moves differently here. Space breathes.

Then you look down. The floor. You've walked on stucco your whole life—you know what it costs. Early temple floors, the ones from your grandfather's time, had limestone slabs over a foot thick. Here, in the palace, the base is still several inches. Solid. But the top layer—the fresh white stucco surface—it's thinner than it should be. Not much. Maybe half an inch less than the older sections near the wall. 

You know what that means. Each square meter of stucco burns through twenty trees. The fuel's running low. They're stretching it thinner.

You move carefully. Nobles pass without looking at you—some areas you simply can't enter, marked by carved thresholds you don't cross. You stay near the edges. Lower personnel like you learn to read the invisible lines: where to stand, where to avert your eyes, when to freeze until someone passes. The spatial grammar of power.

A group of lords walks by, discussing tomorrow's ceremony. They step over that thin stucco floor like it's eternal.

This beauty—this jade, this space, this light—and the plaza where attendance keeps dropping. Same city. The luxury's still here. It's just burning through what's left.

Do they see it? Can they do anything? Or are they walking on that thinning floor pretending it'll hold forever?

CH09.text:
[CH09 | 8:00–8:54 | 王室仪式的盛宴与消费规模目录：用数字与专属性把繁荣推到顶点，为后段的倒计时蓄势]

They're performing permanence.

Tomorrow, the king hosts a katun ceremony—the twenty-year cycle renewal. The lords are gathering. I've seen the supply lists. I know what goes into a ritual this size.

Forty nobles will attend. Each rank has its place: the high lords closest to the throne, the regional governors one tier back, the allied city delegates at the outer ring. Everyone knows where to stand. The seating geometry itself is a political map.

The offerings: two hundred ears of maize, thirty chickens, five pounds of copal resin. That's more copal than my temple district burns in a month. The maize alone could feed fifty families for a week.

But no one at this level seems surprised by forty nobles and two hundred ears of maize. This is normal. This is what a katun ceremony looks like. It's always looked like this.

I walk past the high priest's study. The walls are painted with mythological scenes—gods emerging from the underworld, blood flowing upward into sky-bands. The fire bowls are jade-rimmed. The incense burners are carved in the shape of vision serpents. This is where the calendar is kept. This is where the prophecies are issued.

The king's private altar is behind a carved screen. Only the highest-ranking priests enter. I glimpse it for a moment: quetzal feathers draped over a stone throne, obsidian mirrors catching torchlight, painted glyphs announcing his titles in columns down the walls.

The scale of what's being consumed to maintain this—the trees for the copal, the labor for the maize, the artisans for the carvings—it's all still flowing. Resources are still being pulled from the countryside and concentrated here. The system is still running.

But I remember the simplified offerings in the plaza. I remember what the stone carver said about wood. That disparity—full-scale ritual up here, shrinking supplies down there—it's not sustainable. The numbers don't close.

No one's saying it. But the math is sitting there in the supply lists.

Night falls. The temple summit is lit with torches. From up here, the stars are clean and bright above the forest canopy. It's beautiful. It's silent except for the wind and the distant sound of drums starting up in the plaza below.

This moment feels like permanence. Fire and stone and sky. The way it's always been.

But how long can forty nobles and two hundred ears of maize keep happening when the families who grow that maize are starting to leave?

CH10.text:
[CH10 | 8:54–9:36 | 调性切换与倒计时开启：点名确切日期，从探索模式切换为宿命模式，所有幽默节拍归零]

You stand on top of the pyramid as the sun moves west. The city spreads below you. Smoke from cooking fires. The plaza where a thousand people danced two months ago. The workshop where the altar stone sits.

It is February of 822. Two years ago, on February 10th of that year, the king carved the first side of that altar. One face showing his coronation. That's when the work was supposed to accelerate. This is when the second face should be halfway done. The third and fourth still blank, waiting.

But the chisels haven't moved in two years.

You're the only person in this city who walks past that stone every single day. The only one who sees it not as a monument, but as a timer.

And you're not alone in knowing what the timer means.

Because you're not the only city watching this happen.

In Palenque, the last stone carved with a date was 799.

In Yaxchilán, it was 808.

You. 822.

And across the forest, in Tikal—889. In Toniná—909.

Every major city. Every city with carvers and priests and kings. One by one, the stones stopped. The dates stopped. And each time, the silence after was the same: a region running out of reasons to say it was forever.

This isn't a delay. This is the record ending.

You look at the people in the plaza below. They're still waiting. Still believing the next katun will restore what this one promised. They can't see what you see from up here. They can't see that the very system designed to announce permanence has just announced that permanence stopped.

Now what do you do?

CH11.text:
[CH11 | 9:36–10:36 | 干预计划的彩排与准备：交代所有的情报、机会、说辞与时间限制，让观众与主角一起预演失败]

You decide.

Tomorrow morning, the king holds a ceremony at dawn. It's a standard bloodletting rite—nothing as large as a katun dedication, just the routine maintenance of the cosmic contract. He performs, the high priest attends, a few nobles witness. That's your window.

You've been to these before. You know the rhythm. The king arrives at first light, performs the offering, stays for the morning prayers. There's a moment between the bloodletting and the final blessing when attendants prepare the next ritual object. That's when people approach with reports—tribute tallies, calendar confirmations, upcoming feast dates. You're ah k'in. You have standing to speak.

You lay out your ceremonial headband. Check the jade bead that marks your rank. Smooth the bark-cloth sash. You've worn this a hundred times, but tonight your hands keep adjusting, re-checking, making sure everything signals: I belong here. I have the right to be heard.

You rehearse the words.

"Lord, I must tell you what I'm seeing. The stonemasons say there's no wood left to burn lime. The ritual attendance—last month's ceremony had half the people we expected. And the rains you promised in the planting season, they haven't come."

You try different openings. "With respect, Lord—" No, too soft. "I bring an urgent report—" Too dramatic. He'll dismiss it as panic. You settle on direct: "Lord, three things." Count them on your fingers. Wood. Attendance. Rain. Facts, not interpretations. Let him draw the conclusion.

But you also know what he'll say.

The standard response: "We have performed the rites. We have given blood. The gods do not abandon those who honor them." Or: "This is the natural oscillation of the katun cycle. The next turn will bring abundance." Or the simplest version: "The k'uhul ajaw has spoken to the gods. They have answered."

You've heard these phrases your whole life. They're designed to end doubt. And maybe he believes them. Maybe he has to.

The copal incense you'll burn tomorrow—it makes you lightheaded if you breathe too much. The ceremonial tunic weighs more than it looks. You'll be standing in the heat, already tired from the pre-dawn preparation, trying to hold the king's attention while your vision swims and your shoulders ache under embroidered cotton.

You pack the incense pouch. Twice. Check the calendar scroll in case he asks which date you're concerned about. Confirm the jade bead is secure.

You know this might not work. Kings don't reverse course because a town priest reports bad signs. The inscriptions don't record moments when the system admitted it was wrong. But someone has to say it. Someone who sees the stopped chisel, the thinning crowds, the empty sky has to stand in front of the person whose word is supposed to make the rain come and say: it's not coming.

Tomorrow at dawn. One chance.

Will he listen?

CH12.text:
[CH12 | 10:36–11:12 | 警告被驳回与使命收束：向权力说真话，却得到了克制的拒绝，观众与主角一起体验无力感与和解]

You find him after the ritual, in the corridor between the throne room and the private altar. The brazier smoke is still thick. He's removing the ceremonial headband.

"My lord. I need to tell you something. The stone carvers—they say there's no more wood to burn for lime. The ritual attendance last month was half what it used to be. And the rains you promised for this season. They haven't come."

He doesn't interrupt. He listens. Then he speaks, and his voice is calm, almost kind.

"We have performed the offerings. We have bled for the gods. The covenant does not break because one season is difficult. This is the k'atun cycle—it turns. The next period will restore balance. The gods do not abandon those who serve them correctly."

It's not anger. It's not punishment. It's something worse: a answer so complete it leaves no room for reply. The system already has a script for this. You realize it now—inscriptions don't record doubts because the language of kingship cannot contain them. There's no format for "the gods didn't respond." Only victories get carved.

You tried. That's all a town priest can do. The system isn't designed to hear what you just said. It's designed to absorb it, reframe it, and continue.

But the altar is still unfinished. The chisels are still there. And the countdown hasn't stopped.

CH13.text:
[CH13 | 11:12–12:00 | 倒计时的物理撞击与见证者的独白：时间戳报时、知情独白、目击瞬间、旁观者毫无所觉的对比]

It is 822. February has passed. The altar is still there.

One face shows the king's accession. The second face was begun. Two faces remain blank. The chisels haven't moved.

You walk past it every day. Most people don't look anymore. It's just part of the plaza now—furniture, almost.

But you know what it means.

The stone carvers didn't come back. Not in February. Not in March. Not in the months after. In other cities, the same thing is happening. Up north, people are starting to leave. Not all at once. Not dramatically. Quietly. Families packing what they can carry. Moving toward Yucatan, toward the northern settlements where the water doesn't fail. The archaeology will show it later—a slow drain northward, beginning exactly when you'd predict. Population numbers that historians will spend decades arguing about. But here, now, you just see the gaps.

Fewer people at market. Fewer hands for harvest. Fewer voices in the evening.

You mention this to someone—one of the remaining merchants, maybe, or an elder who still comes to the plaza.

"Perhaps the next rainy season will be better," they say. As if the rains are simply delayed. As if this is a pause, not a stop.

"Perhaps the next katun will bring renewal," someone else offers. Twenty years away. They might believe it. They might not. It doesn't matter. They say it anyway. Everyone keeps saying it.

But you're the only one who knows that no new stelae are being carved. The only one who understands that the end of the inscription tradition means something the inscriptions themselves could never say. The only one watching the altar for proof that the promise has failed.

The chisels are still there. No one has touched them in months now.

CH14.text:
[CH14 | 12:00–12:48 | 官方措辞与真相的落差、数字对比与拒绝面对现实的细节：见证者情绪决堤与崩解独白]

They're still saying it's temporary. Next rainy season will fix it.

But the bones don't agree.

I've been looking at the burials. Lately they show something new—growth lines that stop partway, teeth that didn't develop right, adults shorter than the generation before. It's all the same thing: not enough to eat, year after year. This isn't a bad harvest. This is chronic starvation written into the skeleton.

The royal banquets keep happening. Eleven courses. Intact. But out in the plazas where we hold the rituals? Attendance dropped to half of what it was five years ago. Hundreds used to crowd in. Now maybe fifty show up, and half of them look like they're there because they have to be.

Someone tells me, "The rains will return next cycle." They really believe it. They have to.

But I can't keep pretending. Not anymore. I stand there every dawn announcing the festival dates, marking out the calendar cycles, doing everything I was trained to do to hold this universe in place. And every single time fewer people listen. Every ceremony, the offerings get smaller. Every month, fewer names in the tally books.

The system isn't broken. It's just—stopping. Task by task. And I'm the only one who can't look away.

CH15.text:
[CH15 | 12:48–14:00 | 结尾回扣与主题对照句：用'读过与活过'的终极对照完成全片意义的统合，无CTA克制结束]

I don't have the words. There's no inscription format for this. No stela type that lets you carve "the promise stopped working." The entire system was built to announce victories, dedications, royal bloodlettings—永恒 carved into stone. There's no template for failure. So it just... doesn't get written.

When you read about the Maya collapse in a book, it's a date. Maybe a footnote: "Southern Lowlands population declined over 90% between 800 and 950 CE." One line. A scholarly term. "Classic Period Terminal Collapse."

But when you live it? You walk past that altar every single morning. You see the chisels sitting there, untouched. You watch Chac pack up his tools and leave without saying goodbye. You keep announcing ceremony dates to an empty plaza. You write tribute tallies that no one will ever collect. You keep doing your job—calibrating the sacred calendar, preparing offerings, marking out the k'atun cycles—knowing that fewer people show up each time, knowing the rain still hasn't come, knowing that block of stone will never be finished.

The people who wrote the inscriptions only recorded what kings wanted remembered. And kings don't commission stelae that say "we failed." So the silence itself becomes the record. That unfinished altar? That's the most honest monument Copán ever built.

When you read collapse, you see a number. When you live collapse, you see the empty seat at the ceremony. The supply list that gets shorter every month. The plaza that used to hold hundreds and now holds twelve. The children with bones too thin. The families who left last week without telling anyone.

History gets written by the people with the chisels and the right to carve. And sometimes, the truest history is what they left blank.

一、你是谁：玛雅祭司制度档案（立人设的事实底座）
注意时代差：古典期（约250–900年）祭司制度的直接文献极少，最完整的祭司组织描述来自兰达主教16世纪记录的尤卡坦（后古典期末期）。两者相隔600年，引用时必须标注时代。【争议：古典期是否有独立祭司阶层曾长期争论；近年碑铭研究已确认存在专职祭司头衔】
祭司等级（兰达记录的后古典期尤卡坦体系）【一手：兰达《尤卡坦风物志》】
职位

古典期碑铭中已确认的祭司头衔【同行评审：碑文学研究】
- aj k'uhuun（"圣书之人/掌书者"）：负责记录、谱系、贡品账目与教学；
- yajaw k'ahk'（"火之主"）：主祭火仪式；
- ti' sak huun（"白头带的发言人"）：神谕职能，与后世的chilan对应。
- 祭司多为贵族次子——祭司系统是贵族阶层给"当不了国王的孩子"安排的高位出路。
一个必须知道的设定：国王本人就是最高祭司
- 古典期国王称号k'uhul ajaw（"神圣的领主"），王权即神权。碑铭里国王亲自主持放血、舞蹈、立碑——你的主角"祭司"和王权是同一台机器的两个部件。【同行评审】
- 兰达的记录里，尤卡坦国王（halach uinic，"真实的人"）同时被定义为"统治者"与"主教"。【一手】
二、祭司的工具箱：历法与仪式机器
祭司掌管的历法体系【考古/实物】
- 卓尔金历（Tzolk'in）：260天神圣历，管占卜与仪式择日；
- 哈布历（Haab'）：365天太阳历=18个月×20天+年末5天"无名日"（Wayeb'，瓦耶布）；
- 两历咬合出52年一轮的"历法轮回"（Calendar Round）；
- 长纪历（Long Count）：以公元前3114年为纪元零点的大数计时，碑文里的绝对纪年——古典期崩溃后逐渐停用，后世改用"短历"（卡顿轮）。
无名日（Wayeb'）——祭司每年最紧张的五天【一手：兰达】
- 年末最后五天"不属于任何月份"，被兰达记录为凶日：人们不洗澡、不梳头、不做粗活；炉灶熄火；不出门远行——此时人间与冥界西巴尔巴（Xibalba，"可怖之地"）的边界最薄。
- 同时这又是新年仪式的窗口：村民制作来年值年神的偶像，抬到城郊祭台，献科巴香（copal）、谷物和鸡，舞者踩高跷；值年神每年轮换方位（东→北→西→南）。"时间不会自动延续，必须靠仪式重新锚定世界"——这是祭司存在的全部理由。（德累斯顿抄本中的值年神页面与兰达的记录互相印证。）【一手+考古/实物】
卡顿（k'atun）周期大典——20年一次的国家级仪式【同行评审：埃德蒙森（Munro Edmonson）研究】
后古典期尤卡坦的完整流程（多日连台"仪式剧"）：
1. 绕城游行，通宵饮宴；
2. 新卡顿"就座"——新任卡顿祭司（b'alam，"美洲豹"）登上"卡顿之席"，其神谕发言人（chilam）同场就位；
3. 四位"值年祭司"（b'akab'）就座；
4. 七名祭司"丈量"土地、确认地契、征收贡赋；
5. 清点诸位领主的"席次"（权力座次重新排定）；
6. 献祭、乐舞、宴饮；
7. 最后一天"质询诸酋长"，由神谕祭司宣读下一个卡顿的预言；
8. 集体放血；竖立石碑纪念。
- 兰达亲笔记下：玛雅人告诉他，他们"每二十年竖立一块这样的石头"。【一手】
- 古典期的实证：蒂卡尔为卡顿周期专门建造"双子金字塔广场"（东金字塔=日出/生，西金字塔=日落/死，南侧九门建筑=冥界，北侧露天围墙=天界，内置石碑+祭坛）——把整套宇宙观盖成了建筑。【考古/实物】
石碑的灵魂观（视频里可以让石碑"活"）【同行评审】
- 玛雅人认为石碑有灵：立碑时有"裹布仪式"（k'altun，石碑被布匹包裹如圣物）；碑文里石碑以神灵本尊的身份被"奉献"——碑不是记载仪式，碑就是仪式本身。碑文学家戴维·斯图尔特（David Stuart）说：【一手】"石碑不只是纪念过去的仪式，而是让那个仪式永远持续下去。"
三、血与烟：祭司手里的两样工具
王室放血（ch'ahb）——证据最硬的一套仪式【考古/实物】
- 亚斯奇兰24号门楣（公元709年10月28日，日期刻在楣上）：王后卡巴尔·舒克夫人（Lady K'ab'al Xook）跪坐，把一根穿满黑曜石刀片和鲻鱼刺的绳索从自己舌头上拉过，血滴进脚边篮中的树皮纸；丈夫"盾豹二世"（Itzamnaaj B'alam II）举火把照明。楣上还有雕刻师签名"莫·查克"（Mo' Chaak）——玛雅艺术里罕见的作者署名。现藏大英博物馆，残留红蓝颜料痕迹。
- 25号门楣（同一建筑）：放血之后，纸烧成烟，一条双头"幻视之蛇"（Vision Serpent）从血中升起，蛇口中浮现持矛战士与特奥蒂瓦坎雨神——血是打通人神之门的钥匙。该楣铭文反常地"镜像反写"，原因至今未解。
- 工具箱实物：贵族墓中成套出土鲻鱼刺（黄貂鱼尾刺）+黑曜石刀+盛血碗，碗内残留物检测为人血。【考古/实物】
- 神学逻辑：诸神曾流血造人（玉米+神血造人），人欠神血债；国王王后放血=偿还，以保太阳运行、雨水如期、玉米生长。【同行评审】
人祭与圣井【考古/实物+一手】
- 执行人祭的是低位祭司（ah nakom）；心脏摘除仪式在金字塔顶平台进行，广场万众仰视。
- 兰达亲见记录奇琴伊察圣井（Sacred Cenote）：【一手】"遇大旱时，他们惯于把活人扔进这口井献祭诸神……他们相信这些人并没有死，尽管再未见过他们。他们还投入大量珍宝。"
- 实物印证：汤普森（Edward Thompson）1904–1910年抽捞圣井，捞出金盘、玉器、铜铃、科巴香丸、橡胶球、鲻鱼刺和人骨（各来源数字口径不一：早期统计40余具，现代汇总估计达两百具，含儿童与青年男女；部分骨骼有钝器伤/割喉痕；锶同位素显示部分死者来自远方——【同行评审，数字标注口径不一】）。井底沉积着厚达约5米的"玛雅蓝"颜料层——祭品先涂蓝再入水。
- 相关解读【解读】：献祭沉积集中在低水位期=旱季求雨的 desperation 仪式。
四、神圣契约：这套体系为什么一旱就崩
- 整套政治神学是一条契约链：国王（神圣领主）放血献祭 ↔ 诸神降下雨水与丰收。祭司是这条链上的技术官僚：择日、行仪、立碑、宣谕预言。【同行评审】
- 所以当连续大旱来临（810、860、910年三波，见《玛雅文明衰亡》篇），死的不只是庄稼，是合法性：王许诺的宇宙秩序没有兑现。学者对崩溃后政治形态的解读：北方玛雅潘（Mayapan）抛弃了神王制，改行贵族合议制（multepal，"共同统治"）——神王制没有复活，这就是民众用脚投出的神学区票。【解读：马松（Masson）等学者明确提出"或对神王制失败的回应"，标注为解读】
五、看着它失效：崩溃期的"祭司视角"证据（本篇核心素材）
5.1 碑文停立=祭司失业的考勤表
- 立碑是祭司-国王体系的核心仪式。各城最后一块纪年碑的日期表（详见前篇）：帕伦克799、亚斯奇兰808、科潘822、蒂卡尔889、托尼那909——之后，长纪历立碑传统整个死亡。【考古/实物】
5.2 科潘L祭坛：一座雕到一半的祭坛，就是王朝的猝死证明【考古/实物】
- 822年2月6日，乌基特·图克（Ukit Took'）继位。他仿照著名的Q祭坛订制L祭坛——只雕完一个面，第二个面起了稿，剩下两个面完全是空白。
- 这座"烂尾祭坛"至今立在科潘北球场。石碑学者马丁与格鲁贝（Martin & Grube）的定评：【同行评审】"一列长王的队伍走到了头。"末代王储不是死于政变屠杀的戏剧性场面——是连雕一块石头的资源都凑不齐了。
- 科潘末期的另一块碑文写着"地基之屋的倾覆"（toppling of the Foundation House）——可能是王朝灭亡在铭文里唯一一次拐弯抹角的回声。【同行评审：解读有争议】
- 此后废弃王宫里住进平民，纪念碑石料被村民拆去盖房。【考古/实物】
5.3 塞巴尔（Seibal）：最后的回光返照【考古/实物】
- 830年，在别处都在衰亡时，塞巴尔被外来武士-商人集团（乔塔尔玛雅）扶持"复国"：849年立碑时，蒂卡尔和卡拉克穆尔的国王还出席了仪式——两个老牌超级大国给一个小城站台。
- 849–889年的17块石碑风格混杂着墨西哥中部外来元素，且工艺四十年间肉眼可见地变粗糙——会雕碑的师傅断代了。
- 889年最后一块碑；900年城基本空了；930年彻底废弃。
5.4 最震撼的"无声"：铭文里没有任何末日预告
- 翻遍全部玛雅铭文与图像，没有任何一处预言或记录这场崩溃本身（PBS《新星》明确表述）。【考古/实物：证据缺失】
- 铭文是王权的宣传工具，只记胜利、登基、立碑——没有体裁允许祭司写下"我们的神没有回应"。这个"集体沉默"本身就是最有力的证词。
六、人没了多少："城市空了"的量级证据
- 佩滕核心区：鼎盛期（约700–800年）约300万–500万人 → 950年不足50万 → 西班牙人来时不足5万。中心地带人口塌缩超过90%。【同行评审：居址密度调查估算】
- 人的身体里写着饥荒：崩溃期骨骼出现发育迟滞、牙釉质发育不全、成年身高下降——慢性营养不良的直接证据。【同行评审】
- 湖泊花粉档案：森林花粉几乎被杂草花粉取代（大规模毁林）；人走之后森林才恢复。【同行评审】
- 一个绝妙的微观证据（NASA考古学家塞弗）：灰泥地板越晚越薄——早期地板石板厚逾一英尺，晚期的只有几英寸。烧一平方米灰泥要烧掉约20棵树，燃料见底了，地板只能越铺越薄。【一手：塞弗团队测量】
- 同期北方人口上升——南人北迁，不是整体灭绝。【同行评审】
七、活下来的祭司们：知识阶层怎么把火种带过崩溃
1. 书写系统没有死：抄写员阶层把传统带进后古典期（研究确认两期抄经传统存在连续性）。【同行评审】
2. 《奇兰·巴拉姆》预言书（Books of Chilam Balam）：殖民时期（17–19世纪成书，承载更早传统）用拉丁字母记录尤卡坦语的祭司秘典——13个卡顿轮转一圈约256年，同名卡顿会重演同类事件；西班牙人恰在"8阿豪"卡顿到来，被玛雅知识阶层纳入预言框架解读为"周期中的动乱与外来者"——祭司们用自己的历法消化了亡国。【一手】书中哀悼原文："这是我们苦难的开始，是纳贡的开始，是什一税的开始。"【一手：《丘马耶尔书》】
3. 伊察王国最后的祭司团：孤守诺赫佩滕岛城至1697年的王国，王宫大殿里有一张十二个座位的石桌——十二祭司团。最后的大祭司与末代国王同名不同职（Ajk'in Kan Ek'）。1697年城破时，岛上保存的玛雅书籍被焚——那是已知最后被毁的手抄本。【一手：西班牙档案】
4. 兰达悖论（视频绝佳的反派角色）：修士兰达1562年7月12日在马尼（Maní）主持火刑式焚书，自认焚毁27部书（其他记载称远超此数），外加约5000件偶像；他的酷刑连西班牙同僚都看不下去，被押回西班牙受审（1569年竟被判无罪）。为了自辩，他写下《尤卡坦风物志》（Relación de las cosas de Yucatán，约1566年）——玛雅制度、历法、文字最完整的殖民时代记录，我们关于祭司制度的大部分知识正来自这个焚书者。他记下的所谓"玛雅字母表"被学界当垃圾扔了快四百年，1952年俄国语言学家克诺罗佐夫（Yuri Knorosov）发现那是音节表——焚书者留下的废纸成了破解玛雅文字的钥匙。【一手+同行评审】兰达原话全文可引：【一手】"We found a large number of books in these characters and, as they contained nothing in which were not to be seen superstition and lies of the devil, we burned them all, which they regretted to an amazing degree, and which caused them much affliction."（"我们发现大量用这种文字写成的书，因其中只见迷信与魔鬼的谎言，便全部烧毁。他们悲痛至极，苦不堪言。"）
5. 四部幸存抄本：德累斯顿抄本（78页，金星表与日食表——祭司的天文工作手册）、马德里抄本、巴黎抄本、格罗里埃抄本。1540年西班牙官员索里塔在高地见过的书"记载了他们八百年前的历史"——全没了。【一手】
八、可直接引用的原文
1. 兰达记新年仪式与无名日（《尤卡坦风物志》）：凶日里"不洗不梳、不做劳务"，并详载值年神巡礼流程。【一手】
2. 兰达记圣井：【一手】"Into this well they have had…the custom of throwing men alive as a sacrifice to the gods, in times of drought, and they believed that they did not die though they never saw them again."（"遇大旱时，他们有把活人投入此井献祭诸神的习俗……他们相信这些人并未死去，尽管再未见过他们。"）
3. 兰达记焚书：【一手】全文见第七部分第4条。
4. 兰达记立碑：玛雅人告诉他"他们惯于每二十年竖立一块这样的石头"。【一手】
5. 斯图尔特谈石碑：【一手】石碑"不只是纪念过去的仪式，而是让那个仪式永远持续下去"。
6. 《丘马耶尔书》：【一手】"这是我们苦难的开始，是纳贡的开始，是什一税的开始。"
九、措辞红线（审片清单）

angles.belief: 文明崩溃应该是某一天突然发生的大灾难（像庞贝火山爆发）
angles.claim: 玛雅崩溃是四十年的慢性资源耗竭，祭司每天都知道在发生什么但无力阻止
angles.one_line: 文明崩溃不是一场地震，是四十年雕不完一块石头的慢性窒息
angles.key_fact: 塞巴尔849-889年四十年立17块碑工艺肉眼可见变粗糙；科潘L祭坛822年2月6日雕到一半就永久烂尾；灰泥地板从一英尺厚降到几英寸因为烧一平方米要20棵树（NASA考古学家塞弗测量）
angles.why_watch: 把教科书里的'文明消失'变成一个祭司的工作日志——今年雕刻师死了、明年燃料不够、后年请不起工匠
angles.risk: 需确认塞巴尔碑文工艺退化的具体可视化证据；可能被质疑'慢性死亡'说法过于简化复杂的多因素崩溃

angles.belief: 玛雅祭司精通预言和历法，应该预见并记录了崩溃
angles.claim: 翻遍所有碑铭没有任何末日预告——因为铭文是王权宣传工具，只能记胜利不能记失败
angles.one_line: 掌管时间的祭司没有留下一个字预言末日，因为这套系统不允许他们说
angles.key_fact: PBS《新星》明确表述：翻遍全部玛雅铭文与图像，没有任何一处预言或记录这场崩溃；碑铭只记登基、胜利、立碑——没有文体允许祭司写'神没有回应'
angles.why_watch: 用'证据缺失'作为最大的证据——这个不能说的秘密比任何预言都更真实
angles.risk: 可能被反驳为'只是没保存下来'；'零条铭文'说法需要确认PBS来源的权威性和完整搜索范围

angles.belief: 文明崩溃意味着文化和知识阶层也消失了
angles.claim: 人口虽崩溃90%，但祭司-抄写员阶层把文字、历法、预言系统带进后古典期，甚至用它解释了西班牙人
angles.one_line: 城市空了，但解释世界的人把整套系统带到了1697年——甚至用它解释了征服者
angles.key_fact: 研究确认古典期到后古典期抄写员传统存在连续性；《奇兰·巴拉姆》预言书把西班牙人纳入'8阿豪'卡顿解释为周期中的外来者；伊察王国1697年城破时祭司团仍有十二座位石桌
angles.why_watch: 崩溃不是终点而是转场——看着城市空了的祭司们如何把'管理时间'的工作延续了800年
angles.risk: 时间跨度过长（到1697年）可能偏离'watching cities empty'的当下感；需确认抄写员传承连续性的具体研究来源

facts.content: 科潘城L祭坛（Altar L）由最后一位统治者Ukit Took委托制作，他于822年2月6日登基（一说2月10日）。这座祭坛模仿著名的Q祭坛设计，但从未完成——只有一面显示了国王登基场景，第二面开始雕刻但未完成，另外两面完全空白。L祭坛是科潘最后一座纪念碑，之后再无任何纪念碑被建造
facts.note: 日期有两个版本：R32说2月10日，R33说2月6日（登基日）。R31明确说L祭坛之后科潘再无纪念碑。R35详细描述了祭坛的未完成状态

protagonist.who: 玛雅古典期城镇祭司（ah k'in），负责主持本地仪式、宣告节庆日期、监督纪念碑工程
protagonist.era: 约810–822 CE，古典期晚期崩溃阶段
protagonist.place: 科潘（Copán）或南部低地类似城邦
protagonist.source_role: 泰坦尼克号三等舱乘客，1912年4月
protagonist.mapping: 三等舱乘客→城镇祭司（中层知识阶层）；头等舱→王室与大祭司礼仪区；船长→国王k'uhul ajaw；潜入头等舱→探访王宫区；警告船长→向国王呈报危机；称呼统一第二人称'你'（无性别标记）；1912→820 CE；英语原片→英语新稿

thesis_card.viewer_belief: 文明崩溃是某一天突然发生的灾难性事件，像火山爆发或地震
thesis_card.truth: 玛雅崩溃是缓慢倒计时，每一天都在发生：祭司每天看到仪式观众变少、石碑工程停工、灰泥地板越铺越薄（木材耗尽）、国王承诺的雨从未到来——承诺的永恒变成了刻不下去的沉默
thesis_card.one_line_thesis: 当你是祭司，每天的任务就是维持永恒，而那块822年雕到一半就再也没人碰的祭坛——那才是真正的记录
thesis_card.ending_landing: 你以为崩溃是某一天发生的，其实是每一天都在发生——只有活在里面的人，才看得见那些停工的石头、空掉的广场、不再到来的雨构成的倒计时
thesis_card.differs_from_source_conclusion: 原片结论'读过与活过是两回事'的核心相同，但新稿聚焦祭司独有的视角：你的职责是宣告永恒（立碑、行仪、择日），所以当永恒停止时，你是第一批看见倒计时的人——这是船上乘客视角无法提供的专业化痛苦
thesis_card.contrast: 翻案：观众以为崩溃是某一天的灾难（火山、地震、入侵），真相是每天的任务清单逐项失效——石匠说没石灰、广场上人越来越少、雨季的雨不来、国王下令雕的祭坛再也没雕完
thesis_card.double_standard: 同样面对干旱，贵族仍能获得祭品供奉（考古证据：晚期墓葬中仍有玉器与进口奢侈品），平民出现营养不良骨骼证据（发育迟滞、牙釉质发育不全）；或：祭司继续执行每一个仪式日期，但参加的平民从满广场到寥寥数人
thesis_card.boundary: 不适用于真正突发的灾难（如庞贝火山爆发）；不适用于有明确预警记录留存的崩溃事件；不适用于崩溃后立刻复兴的文明（玛雅核心区人口塌缩超90%且未恢复）
thesis_card.comment_question: 如果你是那个祭司：你会选择继续执行每一个仪式日期假装一切正常，还是公开承认你每天看到的危机？

facts.content: 科潘城L祭坛由最后一位统治者Ukit Took委托制作，他于822年2月6日（一说2月10日）登基。这座祭坛模仿著名的Q祭坛设计，但从未完成——只有一面显示了国王登基场景，第二面开始雕刻但未完成，另外两面完全空白。这是科潘最后一座纪念碑，之后再无任何纪念碑被建造
facts.source: Digital Archaeological Record - Copán II; Sciencenetlinks; DBpedia

facts.content: 南部低地各主要城市最后一块长纪历纪年石碑的日期：帕伦克799年、亚斯奇兰808年、科潘822年、蒂卡尔889年、托尼那909年——之后长纪历立碑传统整个死亡
facts.source: 用户提供参考资料第五部分
facts.region: 南部低地（帕伦克、亚斯奇兰、科潘、蒂卡尔、托尼那）

facts.content: 兰达记录的后古典期尤卡坦祭司体系（16世纪，距古典期崩溃600年）：大祭司ahau can mai世袭多为贵族次子，负责撰书、教授文字历法、考核任命新祭司；城镇祭司ah k'in主持本镇仪式、宣谕节庆日期；神谕祭司chilan发布预言；献祭执事ah nakom地位较低；助手chac四位老人协助
facts.source: 兰达《尤卡坦风物志》，约1566年；用户提供参考资料第一部分
facts.freshness: 时效风险：后古典期末期材料，与古典期820年代相隔600年

facts.slot: 古典期碑铭确认的祭司头衔
facts.content: 古典期碑铭中已确认的祭司头衔：aj k'uhuun（'圣书之人/掌书者'）负责记录、谱系、贡品账目与教学；yajaw k'ahk'（'火之主'）主祭火仪式；ti' sak huun（'白头带的发言人'）神谕职能，对应后世chilan
facts.source: 碑文学研究，用户提供参考资料第一部分

facts.content: 古典期国王称号k'uhul ajaw（'神圣的领主'），王权即神权。碑铭里国王亲自主持放血、舞蹈、立碑。兰达记录里尤卡坦国王（halach uinic，'真实的人'）同时被定义为统治者与主教
facts.source: 同行评审研究+兰达《尤卡坦风物志》，用户提供参考资料第一部分
facts.year: 古典期（碑铭）+16世纪（兰达记录）

facts.content: 祭司掌管的历法：卓尔金历（Tzolk'in）260天神圣历管占卜；哈布历（Haab'）365天太阳历=18月×20天+年末5天无名日（Wayeb'）；两历咬合52年一轮'历法轮回'；长纪历以公元前3114年为纪元零点
facts.source: 考古/实物，用户提供参考资料第二部分

facts.content: 年末无名日（Wayeb'）五天：兰达记录人们不洗澡、不梳头、不做粗活、炉灶熄火、不出门——此时人间与冥界西巴尔巴边界最薄。同时是新年仪式窗口：制作值年神偶像、抬到城郊祭台、献科巴香谷物和鸡、舞者踩高跷；值年神每年轮换方位
facts.source: 兰达《尤卡坦风物志》+德累斯顿抄本，用户提供参考资料第二部分
facts.freshness: 时效风险：后古典期记录

facts.content: 20年一次的卡顿（k'atun）周期大典：绕城游行通宵饮宴、新卡顿祭司登席、四位值年祭司就座、七名祭司丈量土地征收贡赋、清点诸领主席次、献祭乐舞宴饮、质询酋长宣读预言、集体放血、竖立石碑。古典期蒂卡尔为此专建'双子金字塔广场'
facts.source: 埃德蒙森研究+兰达记录+考古，用户提供参考资料第二部分
facts.year: 后古典期记录，古典期有实物印证
facts.region: 尤卡坦（记录）+蒂卡尔（实物）

facts.content: 玛雅人认为石碑有灵：立碑时有'裹布仪式'（k'altun）石碑被布匹包裹如圣物；碑文里石碑以神灵本尊身份被奉献。碑文学家戴维·斯图尔特说：'石碑不只是纪念过去的仪式，而是让那个仪式永远持续下去'
facts.source: David Stuart研究，用户提供参考资料第二部分

facts.content: 亚斯奇兰24号门楣（公元709年10月28日）：王后卡巴尔·舒克夫人跪坐，把穿满黑曜石刀片和鲻鱼刺的绳索从舌头拉过，血滴进脚边篮中树皮纸；丈夫'盾豹二世'举火把照明。门楣有雕刻师签名'莫·查克'，现藏大英博物馆
facts.source: 考古/实物，用户提供参考资料第三部分

facts.content: 贵族墓中成套出土鲻鱼刺（黄貂鱼尾刺）+黑曜石刀+盛血碗，碗内残留物检测为人血
facts.source: 考古/实物，用户提供参考资料第三部分

facts.content: 神学逻辑：诸神曾流血造人（玉米+神血造人），人欠神血债；国王王后放血=偿还，以保太阳运行、雨水如期、玉米生长
facts.source: 同行评审研究，用户提供参考资料第三部分

facts.content: 奇琴伊察圣井（Sacred Cenote）：兰达记录'遇大旱时惯于把活人扔进此井献祭诸神……相信这些人并未死去'。1904-1910抽捞捞出金盘、玉器、铜铃、科巴香丸、橡胶球、鲻鱼刺和人骨（口径不一：早期统计40余具，现代汇总估计达两百具，含儿童与青年男女；部分骨骼有钝器伤/割喉痕；锶同位素显示部分来自远方）。井底约5米厚'玛雅蓝'颜料层——祭品先涂蓝再入水
facts.source: 兰达记录+汤普森抽捞+同行评审，用户提供参考资料第三部分

facts.content: 三波干旱：810、860、910年（参考《玛雅文明衰亡》篇）
facts.source: 用户提供参考资料第四部分引用

facts.content: 政治神学契约链：国王（神圣领主）放血献祭 ↔ 诸神降下雨水与丰收。祭司是技术官僚：择日、行仪、立碑、宣谕预言。当连续大旱来临，死的不只是庄稼，是合法性：王许诺的宇宙秩序没有兑现
facts.source: 同行评审研究，用户提供参考资料第四部分

facts.slot: 塞巴尔最后的回光返照
facts.content: 塞巴尔（Seibal）830年被外来集团扶持复国：849年立碑时蒂卡尔和卡拉克穆尔国王出席——两个老牌超级大国给小城站台。849-889年17块石碑风格混杂墨西哥中部元素，工艺四十年间肉眼可见变粗糙——会雕碑的师傅断代了。889年最后一块碑；900年城基本空了；930年彻底废弃
facts.source: 考古/实物，用户提供参考资料第五部分5.3

facts.content: 翻遍全部玛雅铭文与图像，没有任何一处预言或记录这场崩溃本身（PBS《新星》明确表述）。铭文是王权宣传工具，只记胜利、登基、立碑——没有体裁允许祭司写下'我们的神没有回应'。这个'集体沉默'本身就是最有力的证词
facts.source: PBS Nova（引用但未找到原始链接）+考古/实物：证据缺失，用户提供参考资料第五部分5.4

facts.content: 佩滕核心区：鼎盛期（约700-800年）约300万–500万人 → 950年不足50万 → 西班牙人来时不足5万。中心地带人口塌缩超过90%
facts.source: 同行评审：居址密度调查估算，用户提供参考资料第六部分

facts.content: 崩溃期骨骼出现发育迟滞、牙釉质发育不全、成年身高下降——慢性营养不良的直接证据
facts.source: 同行评审研究，用户提供参考资料第六部分

facts.content: 湖泊花粉档案：森林花粉几乎被杂草花粉取代（大规模毁林）；人走之后森林才恢复
facts.source: 同行评审研究，用户提供参考资料第六部分
facts.year: 古典期晚期至后古典期

facts.content: NASA考古学家塞弗团队测量：灰泥地板越晚越薄——早期地板石板厚逾一英尺，晚期只有几英寸。烧一平方米灰泥要烧掉约20棵树，燃料见底了，地板只能越铺越薄
facts.source: 塞弗团队测量，用户提供参考资料第六部分

facts.content: 同期北方人口上升——南人北迁，不是整体灭绝
facts.source: 同行评审研究，用户提供参考资料第六部分
facts.year: 古典期晚期至后古典期

facts.content: 科潘统治者16号Yax Pasaj Chan Yopaat统治了47年，是这个时代最重要的统治者。在他死后，只有一座未完成的纪念碑（L祭坛）被奉献，展示第17位统治者Ukit Took。9世纪科潘出现大规模人口下降
facts.source: Digital Archaeological Record，用户提供参考资料已核对事实

facts.content: 科潘末期一块碑文写着'地基之屋的倾覆'（toppling of the Foundation House）——可能是王朝灭亡在铭文里唯一一次拐弯抹角的回声。此后废弃王宫里住进平民，纪念碑石料被村民拆去盖房
facts.source: 同行评审：解读有争议，用户提供参考资料第五部分5.2

facts.content: 修士兰达1562年7月12日在马尼主持火刑式焚书，自认焚毁27部书（其他记载称远超此数），外加约5000件偶像。他的酷刑连西班牙同僚都看不下去，被押回西班牙受审（1569年判无罪）。为自辩他写下《尤卡坦风物志》（约1566年）——玛雅制度、历法、文字最完整的殖民时代记录。兰达原话：'We found a large number of books...as they contained nothing in which were not to be seen superstition and lies of the devil, we burned them all, which they regretted to an amazing degree'
facts.source: 兰达《尤卡坦风物志》，用户提供参考资料第七部分第4条

facts.content: 四部幸存抄本：德累斯顿抄本（78页，金星表与日食表——祭司的天文工作手册）、马德里抄本、巴黎抄本、格罗里埃抄本。1540年西班牙官员索里塔在高地见过的书'记载了他们八百年前的历史'——全没了
facts.source: 一手资料，用户提供参考资料第七部分第5条
facts.year: 抄本年代不一，索里塔记录1540

facts.content: 科潘在约800年达到顶峰：贵族阶层有约20座宫殿，每座可容纳约250人（Diamond 2021引述）；822年2月最后一位统治者Ukit Took登基并委托L祭坛；此后无新纪念碑。9世纪出现大规模人口下降（具体数字未找到，但骨骼证据显示营养不良增加）；废弃王宫后来住进平民，石料被拆用
facts.source: Digital Archaeological Record; Diamond《崩溃》2021; 同行评审研究
facts.method: 基于R2、R31贵族宫殿数量（20座×250人≈5000名上层人口）估算上层规模；总人口数据未找到，仅能确认9世纪大规模下降趋势

facts.content: 古典期抄写员/祭司（ah ts'ib, aj k'uhuun）受过多学科教育：数学、天文、占星、宇宙学、人类历史；负责历法计算（260天卓尔金历和365天哈布历的咬合，52年一轮）；抄写谱系、贡品账目、碑铭；教授学徒文字与历法；主持城镇仪式、宣告节庆日期；准备仪式供品（科巴香、玉米、鸡、树皮纸用于放血仪式）
facts.source: 同行评审研究（R6碑文学、陶器研究）；R8历法研究；R10维基百科汇总

facts.content: 玛雅铭文是王权宣传工具，主要记录胜利、登基、纪念碑奉献、神灵降临等正面事件；同行评审研究确认铭文格式与政治等级、王权话语、地区竞争紧密相关；碑文学家指出铭文格式的相互引用反映政治从属关系（如基里瓜H号石碑参照科潘J号石碑）；贵族通过铭文表现拟神化身份展示权力
facts.source: 同行评审研究：R11-R13碑文学与政治话语分析；R14铭文结构研究；R15书写符号学研究

facts.content: 考古学界共识：现存玛雅铭文与图像中没有发现任何预言或直接记录古典期崩溃本身的文字（用户资料引用PBS《新星》节目表述，但原始声明链接未在R19-R20中找到）；R10哈佛确认玛雅铭文无2012末日预言；铭文作为王权工具只记正面事件，无体裁记录失败
facts.source: 用户资料引用PBS Nova；模型记忆待核实原始出处

facts.content: 塞巴尔849-889年间17块石碑风格混杂墨西哥中部外来元素；用户资料称工艺四十年间肉眼可见变粗糙——会雕碑的师傅断代了；R21提到849年10号石碑为'巴洛克风格最动感雕刻'，但后期与早期的具体工艺对比描述未在搜索结果中找到
facts.source: 用户提供参考资料第五部分5.3；同行评审：风格变化研究（具体工艺退化对比待核实）

facts.slot: 国王应对危机警告的话术
facts.content: 基于神王制逻辑推测：当祭司向国王警告危机（木材耗尽、仪式观众减少、雨季未至）时，国王或大祭司的官方应对可能采用神学权威话术，例如'我们已经献祭、已经放血，诸神不会抛弃我们'或'这是卡顿轮转的正常波动，下一个周期会好转'——强调仪式已执行、神权不容质疑、困难是暂时的
facts.source: 基于F05国王即神权、F15神学契约逻辑推测，无直接史料记载

facts.slot: 仪式观众人数变化推测
facts.content: 基于人口塌缩证据推测：值年神仪式或公共祭典的观众人数在崩溃期显著下降——从广场满员（数百人）到寥寥数十人。具体数字无考古记录，但F18佩滕核心区人口塌缩超90%、F19骨骼营养不良、F20人口北迁的证据支持公共仪式参与度急剧下降的推论
facts.source: 基于F18人口塌缩、F19营养不良、F20北迁证据的逻辑推论

facts.content: 古典期玛雅城市采用等级化空间布局：普通民居区、市场/广场区、次级贵族住宅区、神庙区、王宫核心区；祭司和抄书员有通行权但需遵守礼仪协议；空间控制研究表明雕塑、铭文和建筑形式共同控制不同阶层的移动和可及性；最隔离和私密的空间保留给王室和高级祭司
facts.source: 同行评审研究：R26-R30空间与雕塑研究（Parmington 2011《古典玛雅城市的空间与雕塑》）
facts.region: 玛雅城市（以帕伦克为案例）

opening_beats.src_line: Okay, so that is the RMS Titanic. This is Southampton docks on April 10th, 1912
opening_beats.new_line: This is a stone altar. It was supposed to have four carved sides showing the king's glory.

opening_beats.src_line: and I am holding a third-class ticket which cost me roughly the equivalent of $500 in today's money. Obviously, I am going to try to get into first class anyway.
opening_beats.new_line: It has one. The chisels are still sitting there. No one has touched them in two years. I'm a Maya priest in 820 AD, and I walk past this thing every single day.

opening_beats.src_line: For now, third class. Here we go.
opening_beats.new_line: Let me show you what it's like when time stops being recorded.

opening_beats.src_line: In this episode, I used real historical illustrations and photographs of the Titanic in the public domain to turn them into photorealistic worlds. Everything you see is as close as we can get to the real thing.
opening_beats.new_line: Everything you're about to see is reconstructed from real Maya stelae, murals, and pottery in the public domain. I'm using AI to bring them to life as close as we can get to the archaeological evidence. Some details come from 16th-century records—600 years after the collapse—so I'll tell you when we're bridging that gap.

opening_beats.src_line: Enjoy, guys. This was a lot of work.
opening_beats.new_line: This took months to piece together. I hope you see what I saw.

opening_beats.src_line: Just between you and me, I want to get into as many rooms on this ship as I possibly can. First class, the dining rooms, the grand staircase, all of it. I also want to try to talk to the captain about the iceberg. I feel like someone should at least try to say something. Wish me luck.
opening_beats.new_line: Here's what I'm going to do. I want to see the royal palace zones I don't normally enter—the king's bloodletting ceremonies, the elite katun rituals, all of it. And I need to find the king or the high priest and tell them what I'm seeing: the stone carvers say we've run out of trees to burn for lime. Ritual attendance is dropping. The rains the king promised haven't come. I don't know if they'll listen, but someone has to say it. And I want to show you what happens when a civilization doesn't collapse in one day—it collapses every single day, in the tasks that quietly stop.

targets: Let me be honest with you...

hook_promise.shape: 承诺揭示一个被所有历史书忽略的视角：崩溃不是某一天发生的，而是每天都在发生——通过一个内部人（祭司）看到的那些悄悄停止的任务（雕到一半的祭坛、变少的仪式观众、烧不起的灰泥地板）

thesis_card.viewer_belief: 文明崩溃是某一天突然发生的灾难性事件，像火山爆发或地震
thesis_card.truth: 玛雅崩溃是缓慢倒计时，每一天都在发生：祭司每天看到仪式观众变少、石碑工程停工、灰泥地板越铺越薄（木材耗尽）、国王承诺的雨从未到来——承诺的永恒变成了刻不下去的沉默
thesis_card.one_line_thesis: 当你是祭司，每天的任务就是维持永恒，而那块822年雕到一半就再也没人碰的祭坛——那才是真正的记录
thesis_card.ending_landing: 你以为崩溃是某一天发生的，其实是每一天都在发生——只有活在里面的人，才看得见那些停工的石头、空掉的广场、不再到来的雨构成的倒计时
thesis_card.differs_from_source_conclusion: 原片结论'读过与活过是两回事'的核心相同，但新稿聚焦祭司独有的视角：你的职责是宣告永恒（立碑、行仪、择日），所以当永恒停止时，你是第一批看见倒计时的人——这是船上乘客视角无法提供的专业化痛苦
thesis_card.contrast: 翻案：观众以为崩溃是某一天的灾难（火山、地震、入侵），真相是每天的任务清单逐项失效——石匠说没石灰、广场上人越来越少、雨季的雨不来、国王下令雕的祭坛再也没雕完
thesis_card.double_standard: 同样面对干旱，贵族仍能获得祭品供奉（考古证据：晚期墓葬中仍有玉器与进口奢侈品），平民出现营养不良骨骼证据（发育迟滞、牙釉质发育不全）；或：祭司继续执行每一个仪式日期，但参加的平民从满广场到寥寥数人
thesis_card.boundary: 不适用于真正突发的灾难（如庞贝火山爆发）；不适用于有明确预警记录留存的崩溃事件；不适用于崩溃后立刻复兴的文明（玛雅核心区人口塌缩超90%且未恢复）

facts.content: 科潘城L祭坛由最后一位统治者Ukit Took委托制作，他于822年2月6日（一说2月10日）登基。这座祭坛模仿著名的Q祭坛设计，但从未完成——只有一面显示了国王登基场景，第二面开始雕刻但未完成，另外两面完全空白。这是科潘最后一座纪念碑，之后再无任何纪念碑被建造
facts.source: Digital Archaeological Record - Copán II; Sciencenetlinks; DBpedia

facts.content: 南部低地各主要城市最后一块长纪历纪年石碑的日期：帕伦克799年、亚斯奇兰808年、科潘822年、蒂卡尔889年、托尼那909年——之后长纪历立碑传统整个死亡
facts.source: 用户提供参考资料第五部分
facts.region: 南部低地（帕伦克、亚斯奇兰、科潘、蒂卡尔、托尼那）

facts.content: 兰达记录的后古典期尤卡坦祭司体系（16世纪，距古典期崩溃600年）：大祭司ahau can mai世袭多为贵族次子，负责撰书、教授文字历法、考核任命新祭司；城镇祭司ah k'in主持本镇仪式、宣谕节庆日期；神谕祭司chilan发布预言；献祭执事ah nakom地位较低；助手chac四位老人协助
facts.source: 兰达《尤卡坦风物志》，约1566年；用户提供参考资料第一部分
facts.freshness: 时效风险：后古典期末期材料，与古典期820年代相隔600年

facts.slot: 古典期碑铭确认的祭司头衔
facts.content: 古典期碑铭中已确认的祭司头衔：aj k'uhuun（'圣书之人/掌书者'）负责记录、谱系、贡品账目与教学；yajaw k'ahk'（'火之主'）主祭火仪式；ti' sak huun（'白头带的发言人'）神谕职能，对应后世chilan
facts.source: 碑文学研究，用户提供参考资料第一部分

facts.content: 古典期国王称号k'uhul ajaw（'神圣的领主'），王权即神权。碑铭里国王亲自主持放血、舞蹈、立碑。兰达记录里尤卡坦国王（halach uinic，'真实的人'）同时被定义为统治者与主教
facts.source: 同行评审研究+兰达《尤卡坦风物志》，用户提供参考资料第一部分
facts.year: 古典期（碑铭）+16世纪（兰达记录）

facts.content: 祭司掌管的历法：卓尔金历（Tzolk'in）260天神圣历管占卜；哈布历（Haab'）365天太阳历=18月×20天+年末5天无名日（Wayeb'）；两历咬合52年一轮'历法轮回'；长纪历以公元前3114年为纪元零点
facts.source: 考古/实物，用户提供参考资料第二部分

facts.content: 年末无名日（Wayeb'）五天：兰达记录人们不洗澡、不梳头、不做粗活、炉灶熄火、不出门——此时人间与冥界西巴尔巴边界最薄。同时是新年仪式窗口：制作值年神偶像、抬到城郊祭台、献科巴香谷物和鸡、舞者踩高跷；值年神每年轮换方位
facts.source: 兰达《尤卡坦风物志》+德累斯顿抄本，用户提供参考资料第二部分
facts.freshness: 时效风险：后古典期记录

facts.content: 20年一次的卡顿（k'atun）周期大典：绕城游行通宵饮宴、新卡顿祭司登席、四位值年祭司就座、七名祭司丈量土地征收贡赋、清点诸领主席次、献祭乐舞宴饮、质询酋长宣读预言、集体放血、竖立石碑。古典期蒂卡尔为此专建'双子金字塔广场'
facts.source: 埃德蒙森研究+兰达记录+考古，用户提供参考资料第二部分
facts.year: 后古典期记录，古典期有实物印证
facts.region: 尤卡坦（记录）+蒂卡尔（实物）

facts.content: 玛雅人认为石碑有灵：立碑时有'裹布仪式'（k'altun）石碑被布匹包裹如圣物；碑文里石碑以神灵本尊身份被奉献。碑文学家戴维·斯图尔特说：'石碑不只是纪念过去的仪式，而是让那个仪式永远持续下去'
facts.source: David Stuart研究，用户提供参考资料第二部分

facts.content: 亚斯奇兰24号门楣（公元709年10月28日）：王后卡巴尔·舒克夫人跪坐，把穿满黑曜石刀片和鲻鱼刺的绳索从舌头拉过，血滴进脚边篮中树皮纸；丈夫'盾豹二世'举火把照明。门楣有雕刻师签名'莫·查克'，现藏大英博物馆
facts.source: 考古/实物，用户提供参考资料第三部分

facts.content: 贵族墓中成套出土鲻鱼刺（黄貂鱼尾刺）+黑曜石刀+盛血碗，碗内残留物检测为人血
facts.source: 考古/实物，用户提供参考资料第三部分

facts.content: 神学逻辑：诸神曾流血造人（玉米+神血造人），人欠神血债；国王王后放血=偿还，以保太阳运行、雨水如期、玉米生长
facts.source: 同行评审研究，用户提供参考资料第三部分

facts.content: 奇琴伊察圣井（Sacred Cenote）：兰达记录'遇大旱时惯于把活人扔进此井献祭诸神……相信这些人并未死去'。1904-1910抽捞捞出金盘、玉器、铜铃、科巴香丸、橡胶球、鲻鱼刺和人骨（口径不一：早期统计40余具，现代汇总估计达两百具，含儿童与青年男女；部分骨骼有钝器伤/割喉痕；锶同位素显示部分来自远方）。井底约5米厚'玛雅蓝'颜料层——祭品先涂蓝再入水
facts.source: 兰达记录+汤普森抽捞+同行评审，用户提供参考资料第三部分

facts.content: 三波干旱：810、860、910年（参考《玛雅文明衰亡》篇）
facts.source: 用户提供参考资料第四部分引用

facts.content: 政治神学契约链：国王（神圣领主）放血献祭 ↔ 诸神降下雨水与丰收。祭司是技术官僚：择日、行仪、立碑、宣谕预言。当连续大旱来临，死的不只是庄稼，是合法性：王许诺的宇宙秩序没有兑现
facts.source: 同行评审研究，用户提供参考资料第四部分

facts.slot: 塞巴尔最后的回光返照
facts.content: 塞巴尔（Seibal）830年被外来集团扶持复国：849年立碑时蒂卡尔和卡拉克穆尔国王出席——两个老牌超级大国给小城站台。849-889年17块石碑风格混杂墨西哥中部元素，工艺四十年间肉眼可见变粗糙——会雕碑的师傅断代了。889年最后一块碑；900年城基本空了；930年彻底废弃
facts.source: 考古/实物，用户提供参考资料第五部分5.3

facts.content: 翻遍全部玛雅铭文与图像，没有任何一处预言或记录这场崩溃本身（PBS《新星》明确表述）。铭文是王权宣传工具，只记胜利、登基、立碑——没有体裁允许祭司写下'我们的神没有回应'。这个'集体沉默'本身就是最有力的证词
facts.source: PBS Nova（引用但未找到原始链接）+考古/实物：证据缺失，用户提供参考资料第五部分5.4

facts.content: 佩滕核心区：鼎盛期（约700-800年）约300万–500万人 → 950年不足50万 → 西班牙人来时不足5万。中心地带人口塌缩超过90%
facts.source: 同行评审：居址密度调查估算，用户提供参考资料第六部分

facts.content: 崩溃期骨骼出现发育迟滞、牙釉质发育不全、成年身高下降——慢性营养不良的直接证据
facts.source: 同行评审研究，用户提供参考资料第六部分

facts.content: 湖泊花粉档案：森林花粉几乎被杂草花粉取代（大规模毁林）；人走之后森林才恢复
facts.source: 同行评审研究，用户提供参考资料第六部分
facts.year: 古典期晚期至后古典期

facts.content: NASA考古学家塞弗团队测量：灰泥地板越晚越薄——早期地板石板厚逾一英尺，晚期只有几英寸。烧一平方米灰泥要烧掉约20棵树，燃料见底了，地板只能越铺越薄
facts.source: 塞弗团队测量，用户提供参考资料第六部分

facts.content: 同期北方人口上升——南人北迁，不是整体灭绝
facts.source: 同行评审研究，用户提供参考资料第六部分
facts.year: 古典期晚期至后古典期

facts.content: 科潘统治者16号Yax Pasaj Chan Yopaat统治了47年，是这个时代最重要的统治者。在他死后，只有一座未完成的纪念碑（L祭坛）被奉献，展示第17位统治者Ukit Took。9世纪科潘出现大规模人口下降
facts.source: Digital Archaeological Record，用户提供参考资料已核对事实

facts.content: 科潘末期一块碑文写着'地基之屋的倾覆'（toppling of the Foundation House）——可能是王朝灭亡在铭文里唯一一次拐弯抹角的回声。此后废弃王宫里住进平民，纪念碑石料被村民拆去盖房
facts.source: 同行评审：解读有争议，用户提供参考资料第五部分5.2

facts.content: 修士兰达1562年7月12日在马尼主持火刑式焚书，自认焚毁27部书（其他记载称远超此数），外加约5000件偶像。他的酷刑连西班牙同僚都看不下去，被押回西班牙受审（1569年判无罪）。为自辩他写下《尤卡坦风物志》（约1566年）——玛雅制度、历法、文字最完整的殖民时代记录。兰达原话：'We found a large number of books...as they contained nothing in which were not to be seen superstition and lies of the devil, we burned them all, which they regretted to an amazing degree'
facts.source: 兰达《尤卡坦风物志》，用户提供参考资料第七部分第4条

facts.content: 四部幸存抄本：德累斯顿抄本（78页，金星表与日食表——祭司的天文工作手册）、马德里抄本、巴黎抄本、格罗里埃抄本。1540年西班牙官员索里塔在高地见过的书'记载了他们八百年前的历史'——全没了
facts.source: 一手资料，用户提供参考资料第七部分第5条
facts.year: 抄本年代不一，索里塔记录1540

background.how: 祭司日常职责段：用'这套历法比现在的阴历复杂十倍'的现代参照+拆解260天神圣历与365天太阳历的咬合机制，把背景拆成小问题（为什么要两套历法？52年才重合一次是什么体验？），避免干讲制度

midpoint.how: 危机倾诉段（全片约43%处）：换一种不同于前面探索的钩子——用具体细节堆叠（'石匠说树砍光了'+'仪式观众只有往年一半'+'雨季的雨没来'）制造紧张感，这是对FS03任务简报中'观察到的危机迹象'的首次兑现

final15.how: 最后15%：'还有最后一件事——铭文上不会刻的那句话'，回收FS11调性切换时的'只有我知道'，再回扣FS01开场的L祭坛意象，完成'读过vs活过'的主题收束

analysis_original.core_dilemma: 作为祭司，你的职责是维持宇宙秩序（择日、行仪、立碑、宣告永恒）——但当永恒停止时，你是继续执行每一个仪式日期假装一切正常，还是承认你看到的倒计时？选择继续=维护体制但欺骗自己；选择承认=失去职业存在意义且铭文体系不允许你记录失败

candidates.text: Okay, so this is Copán. It's 820 AD, I'm a priest, and I'm walking past the plaza when I see it—Altar L. Two years ago, the king ordered it carved. Right now, only one side is finished. I need to find out when the stone carvers are coming back.

This is a stone altar. It was supposed to have four carved sides showing the king's glory. It has one. The chisels are still sitting there. No one has touched them in two years. I'm a Maya priest in 820 AD, and I walk past this thing every single day.

I'm a priest. It's 820 AD, Copán. My job is to mark time, announce festival dates, and oversee monument projects. The last monument we started is half-carved. The king commissioned it in 822. The stone carvers never came back. Let me show you what that looks like.

opening_beats.src_line: Okay, so that is the RMS Titanic. This is Southampton docks on April 10th, 1912
opening_beats.new_line: This is a stone altar. It was supposed to have four carved sides showing the king's glory.

opening_beats.src_line: and I am holding a third-class ticket which cost me roughly the equivalent of $500 in today's money. Obviously, I am going to try to get into first class anyway.
opening_beats.new_line: It has one. The chisels are still sitting there. No one has touched them in two years. I'm a Maya priest in 820 AD, and I walk past this thing every single day.

opening_beats.src_line: For now, third class. Here we go.
opening_beats.new_line: Let me show you what it's like when time stops being recorded.

opening_beats.src_line: In this episode, I used real historical illustrations and photographs of the Titanic in the public domain to turn them into photorealistic worlds. Everything you see is as close as we can get to the real thing.
opening_beats.new_line: Everything you're about to see is reconstructed from real Maya stelae, murals, and pottery in the public domain. I'm using AI to bring them to life as close as we can get to the archaeological evidence. Some details come from 16th-century records—600 years after the collapse—so I'll tell you when we're bridging that gap.

opening_beats.src_line: Enjoy, guys. This was a lot of work.
opening_beats.new_line: This took months to piece together. I hope you see what I saw.

opening_beats.src_line: Just between you and me, I want to get into as many rooms on this ship as I possibly can. First class, the dining rooms, the grand staircase, all of it. I also want to try to talk to the captain about the iceberg. I feel like someone should at least try to say something. Wish me luck.
opening_beats.new_line: Here's what I'm going to do. I want to see the royal palace zones I don't normally enter—the king's bloodletting ceremonies, the elite katun rituals, all of it. And I need to find the king or the high priest and tell them what I'm seeing: the stone carvers say we've run out of trees to burn for lime. Ritual attendance is dropping. The rains the king promised haven't come. I don't know if they'll listen, but someone has to say it. And I want to show you what happens when a civilization doesn't collapse in one day—it collapses every single day, in the tasks that quietly stop.

thesis_card.viewer_belief: 文明崩溃是某一天突然发生的灾难性事件，像火山爆发或地震
thesis_card.truth: 玛雅崩溃是缓慢倒计时，每一天都在发生：祭司每天看到仪式观众变少、石碑工程停工、灰泥地板越铺越薄（木材耗尽）、国王承诺的雨从未到来——承诺的永恒变成了刻不下去的沉默
thesis_card.one_line_thesis: 当你是祭司，每天的任务就是维持永恒，而那块822年雕到一半就再也没人碰的祭坛——那才是真正的记录
thesis_card.ending_landing: 你以为崩溃是某一天发生的，其实是每一天都在发生——只有活在里面的人，才看得见那些停工的石头、空掉的广场、不再到来的雨构成的倒计时
thesis_card.differs_from_source_conclusion: 原片结论'读过与活过是两回事'的核心相同，但新稿聚焦祭司独有的视角：你的职责是宣告永恒（立碑、行仪、择日），所以当永恒停止时，你是第一批看见倒计时的人——这是船上乘客视角无法提供的专业化痛苦
thesis_card.contrast: 翻案：观众以为崩溃是某一天的灾难（火山、地震、入侵），真相是每天的任务清单逐项失效——石匠说没石灰、广场上人越来越少、雨季的雨不来、国王下令雕的祭坛再也没雕完
thesis_card.double_standard: 同样面对干旱，贵族仍能获得祭品供奉（考古证据：晚期墓葬中仍有玉器与进口奢侈品），平民出现营养不良骨骼证据（发育迟滞、牙釉质发育不全）；或：祭司继续执行每一个仪式日期，但参加的平民从满广场到寥寥数人
thesis_card.boundary: 不适用于真正突发的灾难（如庞贝火山爆发）；不适用于有明确预警记录留存的崩溃事件；不适用于崩溃后立刻复兴的文明（玛雅核心区人口塌缩超90%且未恢复）

facts.content: 科潘城L祭坛由最后一位统治者Ukit Took委托制作，他于822年2月6日（一说2月10日）登基。这座祭坛模仿著名的Q祭坛设计，但从未完成——只有一面显示了国王登基场景，第二面开始雕刻但未完成，另外两面完全空白。这是科潘最后一座纪念碑，之后再无任何纪念碑被建造
facts.source: Digital Archaeological Record - Copán II; Sciencenetlinks; DBpedia

facts.content: 南部低地各主要城市最后一块长纪历纪年石碑的日期：帕伦克799年、亚斯奇兰808年、科潘822年、蒂卡尔889年、托尼那909年——之后长纪历立碑传统整个死亡
facts.source: 用户提供参考资料第五部分
facts.region: 南部低地（帕伦克、亚斯奇兰、科潘、蒂卡尔、托尼那）

facts.content: 兰达记录的后古典期尤卡坦祭司体系（16世纪，距古典期崩溃600年）：大祭司ahau can mai世袭多为贵族次子，负责撰书、教授文字历法、考核任命新祭司；城镇祭司ah k'in主持本镇仪式、宣谕节庆日期；神谕祭司chilan发布预言；献祭执事ah nakom地位较低；助手chac四位老人协助
facts.source: 兰达《尤卡坦风物志》，约1566年；用户提供参考资料第一部分
facts.freshness: 时效风险：后古典期末期材料，与古典期820年代相隔600年

facts.slot: 古典期碑铭确认的祭司头衔
facts.content: 古典期碑铭中已确认的祭司头衔：aj k'uhuun（'圣书之人/掌书者'）负责记录、谱系、贡品账目与教学；yajaw k'ahk'（'火之主'）主祭火仪式；ti' sak huun（'白头带的发言人'）神谕职能，对应后世chilan
facts.source: 碑文学研究，用户提供参考资料第一部分

facts.content: 古典期国王称号k'uhul ajaw（'神圣的领主'），王权即神权。碑铭里国王亲自主持放血、舞蹈、立碑。兰达记录里尤卡坦国王（halach uinic，'真实的人'）同时被定义为统治者与主教
facts.source: 同行评审研究+兰达《尤卡坦风物志》，用户提供参考资料第一部分
facts.year: 古典期（碑铭）+16世纪（兰达记录）

facts.content: 祭司掌管的历法：卓尔金历（Tzolk'in）260天神圣历管占卜；哈布历（Haab'）365天太阳历=18月×20天+年末5天无名日（Wayeb'）；两历咬合52年一轮'历法轮回'；长纪历以公元前3114年为纪元零点
facts.source: 考古/实物，用户提供参考资料第二部分

facts.content: 年末无名日（Wayeb'）五天：兰达记录人们不洗澡、不梳头、不做粗活、炉灶熄火、不出门——此时人间与冥界西巴尔巴边界最薄。同时是新年仪式窗口：制作值年神偶像、抬到城郊祭台、献科巴香谷物和鸡、舞者踩高跷；值年神每年轮换方位
facts.source: 兰达《尤卡坦风物志》+德累斯顿抄本，用户提供参考资料第二部分
facts.freshness: 时效风险：后古典期记录

facts.content: 20年一次的卡顿（k'atun）周期大典：绕城游行通宵饮宴、新卡顿祭司登席、四位值年祭司就座、七名祭司丈量土地征收贡赋、清点诸领主席次、献祭乐舞宴饮、质询酋长宣读预言、集体放血、竖立石碑。古典期蒂卡尔为此专建'双子金字塔广场'
facts.source: 埃德蒙森研究+兰达记录+考古，用户提供参考资料第二部分
facts.year: 后古典期记录，古典期有实物印证
facts.region: 尤卡坦（记录）+蒂卡尔（实物）

facts.content: 玛雅人认为石碑有灵：立碑时有'裹布仪式'（k'altun）石碑被布匹包裹如圣物；碑文里石碑以神灵本尊身份被奉献。碑文学家戴维·斯图尔特说：'石碑不只是纪念过去的仪式，而是让那个仪式永远持续下去'
facts.source: David Stuart研究，用户提供参考资料第二部分

facts.content: 亚斯奇兰24号门楣（公元709年10月28日）：王后卡巴尔·舒克夫人跪坐，把穿满黑曜石刀片和鲻鱼刺的绳索从舌头拉过，血滴进脚边篮中树皮纸；丈夫'盾豹二世'举火把照明。门楣有雕刻师签名'莫·查克'，现藏大英博物馆
facts.source: 考古/实物，用户提供参考资料第三部分

facts.content: 贵族墓中成套出土鲻鱼刺（黄貂鱼尾刺）+黑曜石刀+盛血碗，碗内残留物检测为人血
facts.source: 考古/实物，用户提供参考资料第三部分

facts.content: 神学逻辑：诸神曾流血造人（玉米+神血造人），人欠神血债；国王王后放血=偿还，以保太阳运行、雨水如期、玉米生长
facts.source: 同行评审研究，用户提供参考资料第三部分

facts.content: 奇琴伊察圣井（Sacred Cenote）：兰达记录'遇大旱时惯于把活人扔进此井献祭诸神……相信这些人并未死去'。1904-1910抽捞捞出金盘、玉器、铜铃、科巴香丸、橡胶球、鲻鱼刺和人骨（口径不一：早期统计40余具，现代汇总估计达两百具，含儿童与青年男女；部分骨骼有钝器伤/割喉痕；锶同位素显示部分来自远方）。井底约5米厚'玛雅蓝'颜料层——祭品先涂蓝再入水
facts.source: 兰达记录+汤普森抽捞+同行评审，用户提供参考资料第三部分

facts.content: 三波干旱：810、860、910年（参考《玛雅文明衰亡》篇）
facts.source: 用户提供参考资料第四部分引用

facts.content: 政治神学契约链：国王（神圣领主）放血献祭 ↔ 诸神降下雨水与丰收。祭司是技术官僚：择日、行仪、立碑、宣谕预言。当连续大旱来临，死的不只是庄稼，是合法性：王许诺的宇宙秩序没有兑现
facts.source: 同行评审研究，用户提供参考资料第四部分

facts.slot: 塞巴尔最后的回光返照
facts.content: 塞巴尔（Seibal）830年被外来集团扶持复国：849年立碑时蒂卡尔和卡拉克穆尔国王出席——两个老牌超级大国给小城站台。849-889年17块石碑风格混杂墨西哥中部元素，工艺四十年间肉眼可见变粗糙——会雕碑的师傅断代了。889年最后一块碑；900年城基本空了；930年彻底废弃
facts.source: 考古/实物，用户提供参考资料第五部分5.3

facts.content: 翻遍全部玛雅铭文与图像，没有任何一处预言或记录这场崩溃本身（PBS《新星》明确表述）。铭文是王权宣传工具，只记胜利、登基、立碑——没有体裁允许祭司写下'我们的神没有回应'。这个'集体沉默'本身就是最有力的证词
facts.source: PBS Nova（引用但未找到原始链接）+考古/实物：证据缺失，用户提供参考资料第五部分5.4

facts.content: 佩滕核心区：鼎盛期（约700-800年）约300万–500万人 → 950年不足50万 → 西班牙人来时不足5万。中心地带人口塌缩超过90%
facts.source: 同行评审：居址密度调查估算，用户提供参考资料第六部分

facts.content: 崩溃期骨骼出现发育迟滞、牙釉质发育不全、成年身高下降——慢性营养不良的直接证据
facts.source: 同行评审研究，用户提供参考资料第六部分

facts.content: 湖泊花粉档案：森林花粉几乎被杂草花粉取代（大规模毁林）；人走之后森林才恢复
facts.source: 同行评审研究，用户提供参考资料第六部分
facts.year: 古典期晚期至后古典期

facts.content: NASA考古学家塞弗团队测量：灰泥地板越晚越薄——早期地板石板厚逾一英尺，晚期只有几英寸。烧一平方米灰泥要烧掉约20棵树，燃料见底了，地板只能越铺越薄
facts.source: 塞弗团队测量，用户提供参考资料第六部分

facts.content: 同期北方人口上升——南人北迁，不是整体灭绝
facts.source: 同行评审研究，用户提供参考资料第六部分
facts.year: 古典期晚期至后古典期

facts.content: 科潘统治者16号Yax Pasaj Chan Yopaat统治了47年，是这个时代最重要的统治者。在他死后，只有一座未完成的纪念碑（L祭坛）被奉献，展示第17位统治者Ukit Took。9世纪科潘出现大规模人口下降
facts.source: Digital Archaeological Record，用户提供参考资料已核对事实

facts.content: 科潘末期一块碑文写着'地基之屋的倾覆'（toppling of the Foundation House）——可能是王朝灭亡在铭文里唯一一次拐弯抹角的回声。此后废弃王宫里住进平民，纪念碑石料被村民拆去盖房
facts.source: 同行评审：解读有争议，用户提供参考资料第五部分5.2

facts.content: 修士兰达1562年7月12日在马尼主持火刑式焚书，自认焚毁27部书（其他记载称远超此数），外加约5000件偶像。他的酷刑连西班牙同僚都看不下去，被押回西班牙受审（1569年判无罪）。为自辩他写下《尤卡坦风物志》（约1566年）——玛雅制度、历法、文字最完整的殖民时代记录。兰达原话：'We found a large number of books...as they contained nothing in which were not to be seen superstition and lies of the devil, we burned them all, which they regretted to an amazing degree'
facts.source: 兰达《尤卡坦风物志》，用户提供参考资料第七部分第4条

facts.content: 四部幸存抄本：德累斯顿抄本（78页，金星表与日食表——祭司的天文工作手册）、马德里抄本、巴黎抄本、格罗里埃抄本。1540年西班牙官员索里塔在高地见过的书'记载了他们八百年前的历史'——全没了
facts.source: 一手资料，用户提供参考资料第七部分第5条
facts.year: 抄本年代不一，索里塔记录1540

opening_beats.src_line: Okay, so that is the RMS Titanic. This is Southampton docks on April 10th, 1912
opening_beats.new_line: This is a stone altar. It was supposed to have four carved sides showing the king's glory.

opening_beats.src_line: and I am holding a third-class ticket which cost me roughly the equivalent of $500 in today's money. Obviously, I am going to try to get into first class anyway.
opening_beats.new_line: It has one. The chisels are still sitting there. No one has touched them in two years. I'm a Maya priest in 820 AD, and I walk past this thing every single day.

opening_beats.src_line: For now, third class. Here we go.
opening_beats.new_line: Let me show you what it's like when time stops being recorded.

opening_beats.src_line: In this episode, I used real historical illustrations and photographs of the Titanic in the public domain to turn them into photorealistic worlds. Everything you see is as close as we can get to the real thing.
opening_beats.new_line: Everything you're about to see is reconstructed from real Maya stelae, murals, and pottery in the public domain. I'm using AI to bring them to life as close as we can get to the archaeological evidence. Some details come from 16th-century records—600 years after the collapse—so I'll tell you when we're bridging that gap.

opening_beats.src_line: Enjoy, guys. This was a lot of work.
opening_beats.new_line: This took months to piece together. I hope you see what I saw.

opening_beats.src_line: Just between you and me, I want to get into as many rooms on this ship as I possibly can. First class, the dining rooms, the grand staircase, all of it. I also want to try to talk to the captain about the iceberg. I feel like someone should at least try to say something. Wish me luck.
opening_beats.new_line: Here's what I'm going to do. I want to see the royal palace zones I don't normally enter—the king's bloodletting ceremonies, the elite katun rituals, all of it. And I need to find the king or the high priest and tell them what I'm seeing: the stone carvers say we've run out of trees to burn for lime. Ritual attendance is dropping. The rains the king promised haven't come. I don't know if they'll listen, but someone has to say it. And I want to show you what happens when a civilization doesn't collapse in one day—it collapses every single day, in the tasks that quietly stop.

targets: Let me be honest with you...

hook_promise.shape: 承诺揭示一个被所有历史书忽略的视角：崩溃不是某一天发生的，而是每天都在发生——通过一个内部人（祭司）看到的那些悄悄停止的任务（雕到一半的祭坛、变少的仪式观众、烧不起的灰泥地板）

chapters.fn: 沉浸式开场：第一秒落地时空身位，挂出两条任务线，建立第一人称在场框架
真实性契约与制作说明：声明素材来源、复原方法、时代标注，建立观众对'所见即所考'的信任
任务简报与探索清单：列出祭司的两条行动线，同时暗示中点的两个对比性结局
进入神庙区的阶层检查与日常生活流：用感官细节与现代参照系建立'活人感'，同时展示权力等级制度
与同事/助手的对话与仪式供品清单：用配角的小梦想人化遇难者，预告当晚活动，同时暗示资源消耗
集体仪式高光与小型社群时刻：用归属感与共同体验制造情绪高峰，为后段的崩解蓄能
内部知情者的坦白与危机确认：用私密对话完成'元设定溶解'，锁定观众对危机迹象的第一次完整认知
进入王宫礼仪区的禁入奇观：用阶层对比与材质细节制造视觉冲击，同时加深任务的紧迫感
王室仪式的盛宴与消费规模目录：用数字与专属性把繁荣推到顶点，为后段的倒计时蓄势
调性切换与倒计时开启：点名确切日期，从探索模式切换为宿命模式，所有幽默节拍归零
干预计划的彩排与准备：交代所有的情报、机会、说辞与时间限制，让观众与主角一起预演失败
警告被驳回与使命收束：向权力说真话，却得到了克制的拒绝，观众与主角一起体验无力感与和解
倒计时的物理撞击与见证者的独白：时间戳报时、知情独白、目击瞬间、旁观者毫无所觉的对比
官方措辞与真相的落差、数字对比与拒绝面对现实的细节：见证者情绪决堤与崩解独白
结尾回扣与主题对照句：用'读过与活过'的终极对照完成全片意义的统合，无CTA克制结束

[CH01 | 0:00–0:36 | 沉浸式开场：第一秒落地时空身位，挂出两条任务线，建立第一人称在场框架]

This is a stone altar. It was supposed to have four carved sides showing the king's glory. It has one. The chisels are still sitting there. No one has touched them in two years.

I'm a Maya priest in 822 AD—ah k'in, the one who keeps the calendar, marks the ceremonies, watches the monuments. This is Copán, and I walk past this thing every single day.

Here's what I know: the king ordered this altar carved two years ago. One side finished—the king's coronation scene, perfect detail. The second side? Started and stopped. Two sides completely blank. And those chisels. Still right there. Waiting for hands that never came back.

This isn't just a delayed project. When your job is to maintain eternity—to mark time, to promise the gods that tomorrow will come like today came—a stone that stops being carved is a different kind of record. It's a record of stopping.

I need to go to the palace and find out why. I need to understand what happened to the carvers, what happened to the plan. And I need to tell the king something he probably already knows but won't admit: something has changed.

[CH02 | 0:36–1:12 | 真实性契约与制作说明：声明素材来源、复原方法、时代标注，建立观众对'所见即所考'的信任]

Before we go further, you need to know where this comes from.

Everything you're seeing is reconstructed from real artifacts. Stone reliefs from Copán and other southern lowland cities. Murals painted on temple walls. Pottery decorated with ritual scenes. All of it exists in museums and archaeological records, in the public domain.

The method is straightforward: I take the original relief carvings—the outlines, the figures, the glyphs—and use AI to add color and build the environments around them, as close to the archaeological evidence as we can get.

One complication: some of the ritual details come from a Spanish friar named Diego de Landa, who documented Yucatan Maya ceremonies in the 1560s. That's 600 years after the Classic period collapse. But the basic structure of priest roles and ritual practices seems to have carried through. I'll tell you when we're bridging that gap.

So what does a priest actually do every day? What are the tasks that can stop?

[CH03 | 1:12–1:48 | 任务简报与探索清单：列出祭司的两条行动线，同时暗示中点的两个对比性结局]

As town priest—ah k'in—you announce feast days, conduct rituals, oversee monument carving.

You've been noticing things. Carvers: no lime, trees gone. Ceremony crowds: half. The rains? Didn't come.

Two tasks: see the palace zones. Find the king, tell him.

Will they listen? And how do you get in?

[CH04 | 1:48–3:08 | 进入神庙区的阶层检查与日常生活流：用感官细节与现代参照系建立'活人感'，同时展示权力等级制度]

First: your daily work. You walk into the temple precinct. Copal incense—thick, sweet, almost sticky in your throat. There's your desk: stone carved with calendar wheels, two circles that never quite line up. Tree-bark paper stacked on one side. Red ink, black ink. Today you'll copy tribute lists, check the feast day schedule.

Two calendars run at once. The 260-day Tzolk'in—sacred calendar, for divination, for naming children, for knowing which god holds power today. The 365-day Haab'—solar calendar, eighteen months of twenty days, plus five unlucky days at year's end. They mesh like gears. Every 52 years they click back to the same starting point. That's one Calendar Round. Most people live one, maybe see the start of a second.

This system is ten times more complex than a lunar calendar. You spent your childhood learning to track both wheels, predict their meetings, never let them slip. That's your job: keep the wheels turning.

But here's the thing. The high priest—ahau can mai—he walks straight into the palace. No announcement, no waiting. You? You send word through an attendant. You wait for permission. Same knowledge, different doors. That's how power looks in space.

Today you have ritual work: preparing for the year-bearer ceremony. They'll need you to confirm the date, arrange the offerings.

Your job is to make sure these wheels don't fail. Except they're already failing. And no one with direct access seems to notice.

So: the palace. What does it look like when you finally get in?

[CH05 | 3:08–4:20 | 与同事/助手的对话与仪式供品清单：用配角的小梦想人化遇难者，预告当晚活动，同时暗示资源消耗]

The copal smoke is thick today. Your assistant, Chac, is sorting the bundles on the preparation table—dried corn husks, bound in twine the way they always are. He's humming something, moving his hands with the kind of casual rhythm that comes from doing this a thousand times.

"I was thinking," he says, not looking up. "After I finish helping with the ceremonies this season, maybe I ask for my own posting. A town priest in one of the smaller settlements. My son is learning the glyphs. If I move up, he learns faster. Better teacher, better lineage."

He says it like he's already decided. Like the path is already there.

You hand him the tree bark paper—the white sheets they'll need to catch the blood tonight. Years ago, this stack would be twice as thick. You don't mention it.

"The offerings are ready," he continues, still organizing. "Copal. Corn. Two chickens for the year-bearer ceremony." He taps the bundle. "That should be enough."

Should be. Last month, the high priest's ceremony had twice the copal. The month before that, more. Now it's been cut quietly, no announcement. The supplies get smaller and nobody says why. Chac's eyes have started noticing what his mouth won't say out loud.

You watch him check the inventory. Copal resin in its clay bowl. Corn in its basket. The tree bark paper stacked and ready. The tools for the bloodletting arranged in precise order—the stingray spine, the obsidian blade, the bowl to catch what flows.

"We should move soon," you say. "Change into the ceremonial garments. The ceremony starts before the sun reaches its peak."

Chac nods, rolling the last bundle carefully. He looks at you for a moment—really looks at you, like he wants to ask something but doesn't. Then he glances back at his work.

"Will you come see the new stela I carved? After everything?" He's carved one for the palace courtyard, his first major work. It has the king's face, the date glyph, the usual forms. "It's nothing like what the master stoneworkers did twenty years ago, but... it's what I could manage with what we have."

You promise you will. You both know what that means—if there's anything left to see.

[CH06 | 4:20–5:34 | 集体仪式高光与小型社群时刻：用归属感与共同体验制造情绪高峰，为后段的崩解蓄能]

That night, there's a ceremony in the plaza—one of the year-bearer rituals. The city gathers.

Torches line the perimeter. Drums echo off the pyramid steps. Copal smoke fills the air, thick and sweet, pressing down like the humidity before rain. You can feel the heat of bodies packed close, hundreds of people swaying in rhythm.

The nobles go first. They use stingray spines and obsidian blades—piercing their tongues, letting the blood drip onto bark paper strips laid at their feet. Some of the royal blood relatives do it publicly, right here on the plaza platform. The paper soaks through dark red, then gets rolled and burned in the braziers.

Then the commoners. Most pierce their earlobes—quick, small offerings. A few do their tongues if they're asking for something specific. Everyone bleeds. Everyone participates.

And in that moment, standing in the smoke and the drumbeat, you hear someone say it out loud: "This is our promise to the gods. We bleed, they send rain."

The whole plaza believes it. You can see it in their faces—the certainty, the shared commitment. This is what holds everything together. This contract.

When the ceremony ends and people start to drift away, one of the senior priests—someone you've worked with for years—catches your eye. Doesn't say anything. Just tilts his head slightly toward the edge of the plaza, away from the torches.

You follow him into the shadows between two residential compounds. He waits until the drumming fades and the plaza empties before he speaks.

[CH07 | 5:34–6:56 | 内部知情者的坦白与危机确认：用私密对话完成'元设定溶解'，锁定观众对危机迹象的第一次完整认知]

"The stone carvers," he says. Voice low. "They told you about the trees?"

You nod.

"They told me the same thing three months ago. No trees left close enough to haul. Can't burn lime without fuel. That altar—" He doesn't finish. Doesn't need to.

"It's not just the trees," you say. "Last month's ceremony. The Year Bearer procession. I counted maybe forty people in the plaza. Maybe. A year ago there were hundreds."

He doesn't look surprised. Just tired.

"The rains," he says. It's not a question. "The king promised. We performed the bloodletting. We gave the offering. The year turned over. The rains didn't come."

You both stand there. Not speaking. The contract is supposed to work. The king bleeds, the gods send rain, the maize grows. That's the deal. That's how time continues.

"Tomorrow," he says finally. "The king is holding a private ceremony at dawn. In the palace compound. If you're going to say something—if anyone's going to say something—that's the window."

He meets your eyes. Waits. Then nods once and walks back toward the plaza.

You stand in the dark a little longer. Everything just changed. You're not the only one who sees it anymore. But knowing together doesn't make it lighter. It makes it heavier.

You go back to your quarters. Tomorrow you'll go to the palace. But tonight—tonight you just stand there, looking at the empty plaza, wondering: if we all see it, why are we still pretending the ceremonies will hold? Why can't we just tell the king what's breaking?

[CH08 | 6:56–8:00 | 进入王宫礼仪区的禁入奇观：用阶层对比与材质细节制造视觉冲击，同时加深任务的紧迫感]

You find a reason to enter the palace ceremonial zone—assisting with tomorrow's ritual preparations. The moment you step through, everything changes.

Jade inlay catches the torchlight. Painted stucco—reds, blues, whites—covers every surface in patterns you've never seen this dense. The courtyard opens up three times the width of the plaza you work in. Light moves differently here. Space breathes.

Then you look down. The floor. You've walked on stucco your whole life—you know what it costs. Early temple floors, the ones from your grandfather's time, had limestone slabs over a foot thick. Here, in the palace, the base is still several inches. Solid. But the top layer—the fresh white stucco surface—it's thinner than it should be. Not much. Maybe half an inch less than the older sections near the wall. 

You know what that means. Each square meter of stucco burns through twenty trees. The fuel's running low. They're stretching it thinner.

You move carefully. Nobles pass without looking at you—some areas you simply can't enter, marked by carved thresholds you don't cross. You stay near the edges. Lower personnel like you learn to read the invisible lines: where to stand, where to avert your eyes, when to freeze until someone passes. The spatial grammar of power.

A group of lords walks by, discussing tomorrow's ceremony. They step over that thin stucco floor like it's eternal.

This beauty—this jade, this space, this light—and the plaza where attendance keeps dropping. Same city. The luxury's still here. It's just burning through what's left.

Do they see it? Can they do anything? Or are they walking on that thinning floor pretending it'll hold forever?

[CH09 | 8:00–8:54 | 王室仪式的盛宴与消费规模目录：用数字与专属性把繁荣推到顶点，为后段的倒计时蓄势]

They're performing permanence.

Tomorrow, the king hosts a katun ceremony—the twenty-year cycle renewal. The lords are gathering. I've seen the supply lists. I know what goes into a ritual this size.

Forty nobles will attend. Each rank has its place: the high lords closest to the throne, the regional governors one tier back, the allied city delegates at the outer ring. Everyone knows where to stand. The seating geometry itself is a political map.

The offerings: two hundred ears of maize, thirty chickens, five pounds of copal resin. That's more copal than my temple district burns in a month. The maize alone could feed fifty families for a week.

But no one at this level seems surprised by forty nobles and two hundred ears of maize. This is normal. This is what a katun ceremony looks like. It's always looked like this.

I walk past the high priest's study. The walls are painted with mythological scenes—gods emerging from the underworld, blood flowing upward into sky-bands. The fire bowls are jade-rimmed. The incense burners are carved in the shape of vision serpents. This is where the calendar is kept. This is where the prophecies are issued.

The king's private altar is behind a carved screen. Only the highest-ranking priests enter. I glimpse it for a moment: quetzal feathers draped over a stone throne, obsidian mirrors catching torchlight, painted glyphs announcing his titles in columns down the walls.

The scale of what's being consumed to maintain this—the trees for the copal, the labor for the maize, the artisans for the carvings—it's all still flowing. Resources are still being pulled from the countryside and concentrated here. The system is still running.

But I remember the simplified offerings in the plaza. I remember what the stone carver said about wood. That disparity—full-scale ritual up here, shrinking supplies down there—it's not sustainable. The numbers don't close.

No one's saying it. But the math is sitting there in the supply lists.

Night falls. The temple summit is lit with torches. From up here, the stars are clean and bright above the forest canopy. It's beautiful. It's silent except for the wind and the distant sound of drums starting up in the plaza below.

This moment feels like permanence. Fire and stone and sky. The way it's always been.

But how long can forty nobles and two hundred ears of maize keep happening when the families who grow that maize are starting to leave?

You stand on top of the pyramid as the sun moves west. The city spreads below you. Smoke from cooking fires. The plaza where a thousand people danced two months ago. The workshop where the altar stone sits.

It is February of 822. Two years ago, on February 10th of that year, the king carved the first side of that altar. One face showing his coronation. That's when the work was supposed to accelerate. This is when the second face should be halfway done. The third and fourth still blank, waiting.

But the chisels haven't moved in two years.

You're the only person in this city who walks past that stone every single day. The only one who sees it not as a monument, but as a timer.

And you're not alone in knowing what the timer means.

Because you're not the only city watching this happen.

In Palenque, the last stone carved with a date was 799.

In Yaxchilán, it was 808.

You. 822.

And across the forest, in Tikal—889. In Toniná—909.

Every major city. Every city with carvers and priests and kings. One by one, the stones stopped. The dates stopped. And each time, the silence after was the same: a region running out of reasons to say it was forever.

This isn't a delay. This is the record ending.

You look at the people in the plaza below. They're still waiting. Still believing the next katun will restore what this one promised. They can't see what you see from up here. They can't see that the very system designed to announce permanence has just announced that permanence stopped.

Now what do you do?

You decide.

Tomorrow morning, the king holds a ceremony at dawn. It's a standard bloodletting rite—nothing as large as a katun dedication, just the routine maintenance of the cosmic contract. He performs, the high priest attends, a few nobles witness. That's your window.

You've been to these before. You know the rhythm. The king arrives at first light, performs the offering, stays for the morning prayers. There's a moment between the bloodletting and the final blessing when attendants prepare the next ritual object. That's when people approach with reports—tribute tallies, calendar confirmations, upcoming feast dates. You're ah k'in. You have standing to speak.

You lay out your ceremonial headband. Check the jade bead that marks your rank. Smooth the bark-cloth sash. You've worn this a hundred times, but tonight your hands keep adjusting, re-checking, making sure everything signals: I belong here. I have the right to be heard.

You rehearse the words.

"Lord, I must tell you what I'm seeing. The stonemasons say there's no wood left to burn lime. The ritual attendance—last month's ceremony had half the people we expected. And the rains you promised in the planting season, they haven't come."

You try different openings. "With respect, Lord—" No, too soft. "I bring an urgent report—" Too dramatic. He'll dismiss it as panic. You settle on direct: "Lord, three things." Count them on your fingers. Wood. Attendance. Rain. Facts, not interpretations. Let him draw the conclusion.

But you also know what he'll say.

The standard response: "We have performed the rites. We have given blood. The gods do not abandon those who honor them." Or: "This is the natural oscillation of the katun cycle. The next turn will bring abundance." Or the simplest version: "The k'uhul ajaw has spoken to the gods. They have answered."

You've heard these phrases your whole life. They're designed to end doubt. And maybe he believes them. Maybe he has to.

The copal incense you'll burn tomorrow—it makes you lightheaded if you breathe too much. The ceremonial tunic weighs more than it looks. You'll be standing in the heat, already tired from the pre-dawn preparation, trying to hold the king's attention while your vision swims and your shoulders ache under embroidered cotton.

You pack the incense pouch. Twice. Check the calendar scroll in case he asks which date you're concerned about. Confirm the jade bead is secure.

You know this might not work. Kings don't reverse course because a town priest reports bad signs. The inscriptions don't record moments when the system admitted it was wrong. But someone has to say it. Someone who sees the stopped chisel, the thinning crowds, the empty sky has to stand in front of the person whose word is supposed to make the rain come and say: it's not coming.

Tomorrow at dawn. One chance.

Will he listen?

You find him after the ritual, in the corridor between the throne room and the private altar. The brazier smoke is still thick. He's removing the ceremonial headband.

"My lord. I need to tell you something. The stone carvers—they say there's no more wood to burn for lime. The ritual attendance last month was half what it used to be. And the rains you promised for this season. They haven't come."

He doesn't interrupt. He listens. Then he speaks, and his voice is calm, almost kind.

"We have performed the offerings. We have bled for the gods. The covenant does not break because one season is difficult. This is the k'atun cycle—it turns. The next period will restore balance. The gods do not abandon those who serve them correctly."

It's not anger. It's not punishment. It's something worse: a answer so complete it leaves no room for reply. The system already has a script for this. You realize it now—inscriptions don't record doubts because the language of kingship cannot contain them. There's no format for "the gods didn't respond." Only victories get carved.

You tried. That's all a town priest can do. The system isn't designed to hear what you just said. It's designed to absorb it, reframe it, and continue.

But the altar is still unfinished. The chisels are still there. And the countdown hasn't stopped.
