It is 822. February has passed. The altar is still there.

One face shows the king's accession. The second face was begun. Two faces remain blank. The chisels haven't moved.

You walk past it every day. Most people don't look anymore. It's just part of the plaza now—furniture, almost.

But you know what it means.

The stone carvers didn't come back. Not in February. Not in March. Not in the months after. In other cities, the same thing is happening. Up north, people are starting to leave. Not all at once. Not dramatically. Quietly. Families packing what they can carry. Moving toward Yucatan, toward the northern settlements where the water doesn't fail. The archaeology will show it later—a slow drain northward, beginning exactly when you'd predict. Population numbers that historians will spend decades arguing about. But here, now, you just see the gaps.

Fewer people at market. Fewer hands for harvest. Fewer voices in the evening.

You mention this to someone—one of the remaining merchants, maybe, or an elder who still comes to the plaza.

"Perhaps the next rainy season will be better," they say. As if the rains are simply delayed. As if this is a pause, not a stop.

"Perhaps the next katun will bring renewal," someone else offers. Twenty years away. They might believe it. They might not. It doesn't matter. They say it anyway. Everyone keeps saying it.

But you're the only one who knows that no new stelae are being carved. The only one who understands that the end of the inscription tradition means something the inscriptions themselves could never say. The only one watching the altar for proof that the promise has failed.

The chisels are still there. No one has touched them in months now.

They're still saying it's temporary. Next rainy season will fix it.

But the bones don't agree.

I've been looking at the burials. Lately they show something new—growth lines that stop partway, teeth that didn't develop right, adults shorter than the generation before. It's all the same thing: not enough to eat, year after year. This isn't a bad harvest. This is chronic starvation written into the skeleton.

The royal banquets keep happening. Eleven courses. Intact. But out in the plazas where we hold the rituals? Attendance dropped to half of what it was five years ago. Hundreds used to crowd in. Now maybe fifty show up, and half of them look like they're there because they have to be.

Someone tells me, "The rains will return next cycle." They really believe it. They have to.

But I can't keep pretending. Not anymore. I stand there every dawn announcing the festival dates, marking out the calendar cycles, doing everything I was trained to do to hold this universe in place. And every single time fewer people listen. Every ceremony, the offerings get smaller. Every month, fewer names in the tally books.

The system isn't broken. It's just—stopping. Task by task. And I'm the only one who can't look away.

[CH15 | 12:48–14:00 | 结尾回扣与主题对照句：用'读过与活过'的终极对照完成全片意义的统合，无CTA克制结束]

I don't have the words. There's no inscription format for this. No stela type that lets you carve "the promise stopped working." The entire system was built to announce victories, dedications, royal bloodlettings—永恒 carved into stone. There's no template for failure. So it just... doesn't get written.

When you read about the Maya collapse in a book, it's a date. Maybe a footnote: "Southern Lowlands population declined over 90% between 800 and 950 CE." One line. A scholarly term. "Classic Period Terminal Collapse."

But when you live it? You walk past that altar every single morning. You see the chisels sitting there, untouched. You watch Chac pack up his tools and leave without saying goodbye. You keep announcing ceremony dates to an empty plaza. You write tribute tallies that no one will ever collect. You keep doing your job—calibrating the sacred calendar, preparing offerings, marking out the k'atun cycles—knowing that fewer people show up each time, knowing the rain still hasn't come, knowing that block of stone will never be finished.

The people who wrote the inscriptions only recorded what kings wanted remembered. And kings don't commission stelae that say "we failed." So the silence itself becomes the record. That unfinished altar? That's the most honest monument Copán ever built.

When you read collapse, you see a number. When you live collapse, you see the empty seat at the ceremony. The supply list that gets shorter every month. The plaza that used to hold hundreds and now holds twelve. The children with bones too thin. The families who left last week without telling anyone.

History gets written by the people with the chisels and the right to carve. And sometimes, the truest history is what they left blank.

[CH01 | 0:00–0:36 | 沉浸式开场：第一秒落地时空身位，挂出两条任务线，建立第一人称在场框架]

This is a stone altar. It was supposed to have four carved sides showing the king's glory. It has one. The chisels are still sitting there. No one has touched them in two years.

I'm a Maya priest in 822 AD—ah k'in, the one who keeps the calendar, marks the ceremonies, watches the monuments. This is Copán, and I walk past this thing every single day.

Here's what I know: the king ordered this altar carved two years ago. One side finished—the king's coronation scene, perfect detail. The second side? Started and stopped. Two sides completely blank. And those chisels. Still right there. Waiting for hands that never came back.

This isn't just a delayed project. When your job is to maintain eternity—to mark time, to promise the gods that tomorrow will come like today came—a stone that stops being carved is a different kind of record. It's a record of stopping.

I need to go to the palace and find out why. I need to understand what happened to the carvers, what happened to the plan. And I need to tell the king something he probably already knows but won't admit: something has changed.

[CH02 | 0:36–1:12 | 真实性契约与制作说明：声明素材来源、复原方法、时代标注，建立观众对'所见即所考'的信任]

Everything you're seeing is reconstructed from real artifacts—stone reliefs, murals, pottery. Public domain. AI adds color and builds environments, close as possible to archaeological evidence.

One complication: some ritual details come from 1560s records, 600 years later. I'll tell you when we're bridging that gap.

What does a priest do daily? What tasks can stop?

[CH03 | 1:12–1:48 | 任务简报与探索清单：列出祭司的两条行动线，同时暗示中点的两个对比性结局]

As town priest—ah k'in—you announce feast days, conduct rituals, oversee monument carving.

You've noticed things. Carvers say no lime, trees gone. Ceremony crowds half. Rains didn't come.

Two tasks: see the palace zones. Find the king, tell him.

Will they listen? Let's start with your daily work.

[CH04 | 1:48–3:08 | 进入神庙区的阶层检查与日常生活流：用感官细节与现代参照系建立'活人感'，同时展示权力等级制度]

Temple precinct. Copal incense thick in your throat. Your desk: stone carved with calendar wheels. Tree-bark paper, red and black ink. You copy tribute lists, check feast days.

Two calendars run at once. 260-day Tzolk'in, sacred calendar. 365-day Haab'—eighteen months of twenty days, plus five unlucky days. They mesh like gears. Every 52 years they return to the same point. One Calendar Round.

Ten times more complex than a lunar calendar. Your job: keep them turning.

The high priest walks straight into the palace. You? Send word through an attendant. Wait. Same knowledge, different doors.

Today: preparing for year-bearer ceremony. Confirm date, arrange offerings.

Your job is keeping these wheels from failing. They're already failing. No one with direct access notices.

[CH05 | 3:08–4:20 | 与同事/助手的对话与仪式供品清单：用配角的小梦想人化遇难者，预告当晚活动，同时暗示资源消耗]

Copal smoke thick. Your assistant sorting bundles—corn, twine.

"After this season, maybe I ask for my own posting. Town priest somewhere smaller. My son's learning glyphs."

He says it like the path is already there.

You hand him tree bark paper for tonight's blood offering. Years ago, this stack would be twice as thick.

"Offerings ready. Copal. Corn. Two chickens."

Last month, the high priest's ceremony had more. Now quietly cut. Nobody says why.

"We should change into ceremonial garments soon."

He looks at you like he wants to ask something. Doesn't.

"Will you see the new stela I carved?" His first major work. "Not like the masters did twenty years ago, but... what I could manage."

You promise you will.

[CH06 | 4:20–5:34 | 集体仪式高光与小型社群时刻：用归属感与共同体验制造情绪高峰，为后段的崩解蓄能]

That night, ceremony in the plaza. Year-bearer ritual. City gathers.

Torches. Drums echo off pyramid steps. Copal smoke. Heat of bodies swaying in rhythm.

Nobles first. Stingray spines, obsidian blades—piercing tongues, blood dripping onto bark paper. Some do it publicly here. Paper soaks dark red, gets burned in braziers.

Then commoners. Most pierce earlobes. A few do tongues. Everyone bleeds.

Someone says it: "This is our promise. We bleed, they send rain."

The whole plaza believes it. Certainty. Shared commitment.

When ceremony ends, a senior priest catches your eye. Tilts his head toward the edge, away from torches.

You follow into shadows. He waits until drumming fades.

[CH07 | 5:34–6:56 | 内部知情者的坦白与危机确认：用私密对话完成'元设定溶解'，锁定观众对危机迹象的第一次完整认知]

"Stone carvers," he says. "They told you about the trees?"

You nod.

"Told me the same three months ago. No trees close enough. Can't burn lime without fuel. That altar—"

"Not just trees," you say. "Last month's ceremony. Maybe forty people. A year ago? Hundreds."

He doesn't look surprised. Just tired.

"The rains. King promised. We performed the bloodletting. Gave the offering. Year turned over. Rains didn't come."

You both stand there. The contract is supposed to work. King bleeds, gods send rain, maize grows. That's how time continues.

"Tomorrow. King holds ceremony at dawn. Palace compound. If you're going to say something, that's the window."

He meets your eyes. Nods once. Walks back.

You stand in the dark. You're not the only one who sees it. But knowing together doesn't make it lighter.

Tomorrow you'll go to the palace.

[CH08 | 6:56–8:00 | 进入王宫礼仪区的禁入奇观：用阶层对比与材质细节制造视觉冲击，同时加深任务的紧迫感]

You enter the palace ceremonial zone—assisting with ritual preparations.

Everything changes.

Jade inlay catches torchlight. Painted stucco—reds, blues, whites—dense patterns everywhere. Courtyard three times wider than your plaza.

You look down. The floor. Early temple floors had limestone slabs over a foot thick. Here, the top layer is thinner than it should be. Half an inch less than older sections.

You know what that means. Each square meter burns twenty trees. Fuel's running low. They're stretching it thinner.

Nobles pass without looking. You stay near edges. Learn where to stand, where to avert eyes.

Lords walk by discussing tomorrow's ceremony. They step over that thinning floor like it's eternal.

This beauty—and the plaza where attendance drops. Same city. Luxury still here, burning through what's left.

[CH09 | 8:00–8:54 | 王室仪式的盛宴与消费规模目录：用数字与专属性把繁荣推到顶点，为后段的倒计时蓄势]

They're performing permanence.

Tomorrow, katun ceremony—twenty-year cycle renewal. Lords gathering.

Nobles from allied cities, regional governors. Everyone knows where to stand. Seating geometry is a political map.

Offerings: copal resin, more than your temple burns in a month. Maize that could feed families for weeks.

No one seems surprised. This is normal. Always has been.

High priest's study. Walls painted with gods from underworld. Fire bowls jade-rimmed. This is where the calendar is kept.

King's private altar behind carved screen. Quetzal feathers, obsidian mirrors.

Resources pulled from countryside, concentrated here. System still running.

But you remember simplified offerings in the plaza. What the carver said about wood. Not sustainable.

[CH10 | 8:54–9:36 | 调性切换与倒计时开启：点名确切日期，从探索模式切换为宿命模式，所有幽默节拍归零]

You stand on the pyramid. City spreads below.

February 822. Two years ago, king carved the first altar side. Work was supposed to accelerate. Second face should be halfway done. Third and fourth still blank.

Chisels haven't moved in two years.

You're the only one who walks past that stone every day. The only one who sees it as a timer.

Palenque: last stone, 799. Yaxchilán: 808. You: 822. Tikal: 889. Toniná: 909.

Every major city. One by one, stones stopped.

This isn't delay. This is the record ending.

People below still waiting. Still believing the next katun will restore everything.

[CH11 | 9:36–10:36 | 干预计划的彩排与准备：交代所有的情报、机会、说辞与时间限制，让观众与主角一起预演失败]

You decide.

Tomorrow morning, king holds ceremony at dawn. Standard bloodletting. That's your window.

You know the rhythm. King arrives first light, performs offering. Between bloodletting and final blessing, people approach with reports. You're ah k'in. You have standing.

You rehearse.

"Lord, three things. Stonemasons say no wood left for lime. Ritual attendance last month—half expected. Rains you promised. They haven't come."

You try different openings. Settle on direct. Facts, not interpretations.

But you know what he'll say. "We performed the rites. Gave blood. Gods do not abandon those who honor them." Or: "This is katun cycle oscillation. Next turn brings abundance."

Phrases designed to end doubt.

You pack the incense pouch. Twice. Check calendar scroll.

Someone has to say it.

Tomorrow at dawn.

[CH12 | 10:36–11:12 | 警告被驳回与使命收束：向权力说真话，却得到了克制的拒绝，观众与主角一起体验无力感与和解]

You find him after ritual. Corridor between throne room and private altar. He's removing ceremonial headband.

"My lord. Three things. No more wood for lime. Ritual attendance half what it was. Rains you promised. They haven't come."

He listens. Then speaks, voice calm.

"We performed the offerings. Bled for the gods. Covenant does not break because one season is difficult. This is k'atun cycle. It turns. Next period restores balance."

An answer so complete it leaves no room for reply. System has a script for this. Inscriptions don't record doubts.

You tried.

But the altar is still unfinished. Chisels still there. Countdown hasn't stopped.

[CH13 | 11:12–12:00 | 倒计时的物理撞击与见证者的独白：时间戳报时、知情独白、目击瞬间、旁观者毫无所觉的对比]

822. February passed. Altar still there.

One face shows king's accession. Second begun. Two blank. Chisels haven't moved.

You walk past it every day. Most don't look anymore.

Carvers didn't come back. Not in February. Not March. Not after. In other cities, same thing. Up north, people leaving. Quietly. Moving toward Yucatan, where water doesn't fail.

Fewer people at market. Fewer hands for harvest.

Someone says, "Perhaps next rainy season will be better." As if this is a pause, not a stop.

"Perhaps next katun." Twenty years away.

But you're the only one who knows no new stelae are being carved.

Chisels still there.

[CH14 | 12:00–12:48 | 官方措辞与真相的落差、数字对比与拒绝面对现实的细节：见证者情绪决堤与崩解独白]

They're still saying it's temporary.

But bones don't agree. Burials show growth lines stopped partway, teeth underdeveloped, adults shorter. Chronic starvation written into skeleton.

Royal ceremonies keep happening. But plaza rituals? Attendance dropped to half what it was five years ago. Hundreds used to come. Now fifty, half look like they have to be there.

"Rains will return next cycle." They believe it. They have to.

I can't keep pretending. Every dawn I announce festival dates, mark calendar cycles. Every time fewer listen. Offerings get smaller. Fewer names in tally books.

System isn't broken. It's just stopping. Task by task.

[CH15 | 12:48–14:00 | 结尾回扣与主题对照句：用'读过与活过'的终极对照完成全片意义的统合，无CTA克制结束]

I don't have the words. No inscription format for this. No stela type that lets you carve "the promise stopped working." System was built to announce victories—permanence carved into stone. No template for failure. So it doesn't get written.

When you read about Maya collapse, it's a date. A footnote: "Southern Lowlands population declined over 90%." One line.

But when you live it? You walk past that altar every morning. See chisels untouched. Watch your assistant leave without goodbye. Keep announcing ceremony dates to empty plaza. Write tallies no one collects. Keep calibrating sacred calendar—knowing fewer show up, knowing rain hasn't come, knowing that stone will never be finished.

People who wrote inscriptions only recorded what kings wanted remembered. Kings don't commission stelae saying "we failed." So silence becomes the record. That unfinished altar? That's the most honest monument Copán ever built.

When you read collapse, you see a number. When you live collapse, you see the empty seat. Supply list getting shorter. Plaza that held hundreds now holds twelve. Children with bones too thin. Families who left without telling anyone.

History gets written by people with chisels and the right to carve. Sometimes, the truest history is what they left blank.

I don't have words for this. No inscription format allows it. No stela type lets you carve "the promise stopped." System records victories. No template for failure.

When you read Maya collapse, it's a date. "Southern Lowlands population declined over 90%." One line.

When you live it? You walk past that altar every morning. Chisels untouched. Watch your assistant leave without goodbye.

Like those stelae—Palenque, Yaxchilán, Copán, one by one they stopped. Sometimes, the truest history is what they left blank.

That unfinished altar? The most honest monument Copán ever built.

When you read collapse, you see a number. When you live collapse, you see the empty seat. The work continues. Calendar turns. No one reads it.

versions.text:
[CH01 | 0:00–0:36 | 沉浸式开场：第一秒落地时空身位，挂出两条任务线，建立第一人称在场框架]

This is a stone altar. It was supposed to have four carved sides showing the king's glory. It has one. The chisels are still sitting there. The work stopped after the king commissioned it.

I'm a Maya priest in 822 AD—ah k'in, the one who keeps the calendar, marks the ceremonies, watches the monuments. This is Copán, and I walk past this thing every single day.

Here's what I know: the king ordered this altar carved two years ago. One side finished—the king's coronation scene, perfect detail. The second side? Started and stopped. Two sides completely blank. And those chisels. Still right there. Waiting for hands that never came back.

This isn't just a delayed project. When your job is to maintain eternity—to mark time, to promise the gods that tomorrow will come like today came—a stone that stops being carved is a different kind of record. It's a record of stopping.

I need to go to the palace and find out why. I need to understand what happened to the carvers, what happened to the plan. And I need to tell the king something he probably already knows but won't admit: something has changed.

[CH02 | 0:36–1:12 | 真实性契约与制作说明：声明素材来源、复原方法、时代标注，建立观众对'所见即所考'的信任]

Everything you're seeing is reconstructed from public-domain Maya reliefs, murals, and pottery. AI adds color and settings, guided by the archaeological evidence.

One complication: some ritual details come from 16th century records, 600 years later. I'll tell you when we're bridging that gap.

[CH03 | 1:12–1:48 | 任务简报与探索清单：列出祭司的两条行动线，同时暗示中点的两个对比性结局]

As town priest—ah k'in—you announce feast days, conduct rituals, oversee monument carving.

You've noticed things. Carvers say no lime, trees gone. Ceremony crowds half. Rains didn't come.

Your day begins with the calendar.

[CH04 | 1:48–3:08 | 进入神庙区的阶层检查与日常生活流：用感官细节与现代参照系建立'活人感'，同时展示权力等级制度]

Temple precinct. Copal incense thick in your throat. Your desk: stone carved with calendar wheels. Tree-bark paper, red and black ink. You copy tribute lists, check feast days.

Two calendars run at once. 260-day Tzolk'in, sacred calendar. 365-day Haab'—eighteen months of twenty days, plus five unlucky days. They mesh like gears. Every 52 years they return to the same point. One Calendar Round.

One tracks sacred days; the other tracks the solar year. Your work is to calculate dates and announce the right ceremonies.

A senior court priest can enter palace spaces more directly. You send word through an attendant and wait. The city gives different ranks different access.

Today: preparing for year-bearer ceremony. Confirm date, arrange offerings.

Your job is keeping these wheels from failing. The calendar wheels turn; you check the feast days and prepare the offerings. No one with direct access notices.

[CH05 | 3:08–4:20 | 与同事/助手的对话与仪式供品清单：用配角的小梦想人化遇难者，预告当晚活动，同时暗示资源消耗]

Copal smoke hangs thick as your assistant sorts bundles of corn and twine.

"After this season, maybe I ask for my own posting. Town priest somewhere smaller. My son's learning glyphs."

He says it like the path is already there.

You hand him bark paper for tonight's offering. Its surface is smooth on one side and fibrous on the other; you feel the ridges as you turn it over.

"Offerings ready. Copal. Corn. Two chickens."

You have heard that offerings are being reduced. No one says why.

"We should change into ceremonial garments soon."

He looks at you like he wants to ask something. Doesn't.

"Will you see the new stela I carved?" His first major work. "Not like the masters did twenty years ago, but... what I could manage."

You promise you will.

[CH06 | 4:20–5:34 | 集体仪式高光与小型社群时刻：用归属感与共同体验制造情绪高峰，为后段的崩解蓄能]

That night, ceremony in the plaza. Year-bearer ritual. City gathers.

Torches. Drums echo off pyramid steps. Copal smoke. Heat of bodies swaying in rhythm.

Nobles first. Stingray spines, obsidian blades—piercing tongues, blood dripping onto bark paper. Some do it publicly here. Paper soaks dark red, gets burned in braziers.

Then commoners. Most pierce earlobes. A few do tongues. Everyone bleeds.

Someone says it: "This is our promise. We bleed, they send rain."

You want to believe it too. For a moment, the shared ritual makes the promise feel real.

When the ceremony ends, the senior priest who taught you the calendar catches your eye and nods toward the edge of the plaza, away from the torches.

You follow into shadows. He waits until drumming fades.

[CH07 | 5:34–6:56 | 内部知情者的坦白与危机确认：用私密对话完成'元设定溶解'，锁定观众对危机迹象的第一次完整认知]

"Stone carvers," he says. "They told you about the trees?"

You nod.

"Told me three months ago. No trees close enough. Can't burn lime."

"Last month's ceremony. Far fewer came. A year ago, the plaza was full."

He doesn't look surprised.

"The rites ask for rain. We made the offerings, and the rains have been poor."

You both stand there. The contract is supposed to work. King bleeds, gods send rain.

"Tomorrow. King holds ceremony at dawn. Palace compound. That's the window."

He walks back. You're not the only one who sees it.

[CH08 | 6:56–8:00 | 进入王宫礼仪区的禁入奇观：用阶层对比与材质细节制造视觉冲击，同时加深任务的紧迫感]

You enter the palace ceremonial zone—assisting with ritual preparations.

Jade inlay catches the torchlight, and painted stucco carries reds, blues, and whites. The palace surfaces are more richly finished than the spaces you know at home.

Nobles pass without looking. You stay near edges.

Lords discussing tomorrow's ceremony step over that thinning floor like it's eternal.

You feel the contrast sharply: this palace is still finished and bright, while the public work outside stands unfinished.

[CH09 | 8:00–8:54 | 王室仪式的盛宴与消费规模目录：用数字与专属性把繁荣推到顶点，为后段的倒计时蓄势]

They're performing permanence.

Tomorrow, katun ceremony—twenty-year cycle renewal. Lords gathering.

The nobles know where to stand. Their places mark rank.

The offerings include copal resin and maize, gathered for the ceremony.

No one seems surprised. This is normal. Always has been.

High priest's study. Walls painted with gods from underworld. Fire bowls jade-rimmed. This is where the calendar is kept.

The king's private altar sits behind a carved screen.

But you remember the reduced offerings in the plaza: copal, corn, and two chickens, where there were once feasts. What the carver said about wood. Not sustainable.

[CH10 | 8:54–9:36 | 调性切换与倒计时开启：点名确切日期，从探索模式切换为宿命模式，所有幽默节拍归零]

You stand on pyramid. City below.

In 822, Ukit Took took the throne and commissioned the altar. One face was completed; work on the next stopped.

You pass it every day, and you begin to read its unfinished faces as a measure of what has stopped.

Palenque: 799. Yaxchilán: 808. Copán: 822. Tikal: 889. Toniná: 909.

Across the region, the dated monument record ends at different times.

People below still believing next katun restores everything.

[CH11 | 9:36–10:36 | 干预计划的彩排与准备：交代所有的情报、机会、说辞与时间限制，让观众与主角一起预演失败]

The king's ceremony is at dawn. If you are going to speak, it has to be before or during the rites.

You rehearse the three signs, turning the words over before you speak. You check the incense pouch again.

You know what he'll say. "We performed the rites. Gods do not abandon those who honor them."

Phrases designed to end doubt.

You pack incense pouch. Check calendar scroll.

Someone has to say it.

[CH12 | 10:36–11:12 | 警告被驳回与使命收束：向权力说真话，却得到了克制的拒绝，观众与主角一起体验无力感与和解]

You find him after ritual. Corridor between throne room and altar.

"My lord. No wood for lime. Attendance half. Rains you promised haven't come."

I tell him what we both know: the wood, the crowds, the rain. He listens, his expression calm, then speaks.

"The offerings are made. We have bled. The gods do not abandon those who honor them. This hard season will pass."

He answers with the assurance the court can offer: the rites have been performed, and order will return.

You have said what you came to say. The altar is still unfinished.

[CH13 | 11:12–12:00 | 倒计时的物理撞击与见证者的独白：时间戳报时、知情独白、目击瞬间、旁观者毫无所觉的对比]

You walk past the unfinished altar daily.

You walk past daily. Most don't look anymore.

Carvers didn't return. Not February. Not March. Not after. You walk past daily, and the chisels gather dust; the cuts in the stone do not change.

Someone says, "Perhaps next rainy season." As if this is pause, not stop.

Later, no new monument is built at Copán.

[CH14 | 12:00–12:48 | 官方措辞与真相的落差、数字对比与拒绝面对现实的细节：见证者情绪决堤与崩解独白]

They're still saying it's temporary.

But bones don't agree. Burials show growth lines stopped, teeth underdeveloped, adults shorter. Chronic starvation in skeleton.

One possibility is that public ceremonies drew fewer people as populations declined. No surviving record gives us a reliable count for Copán's plaza.

The public message may still promise that order will return.

As the calendar-keeper, my duty is to maintain these cycles. But every dawn I announce festival dates, fewer listen. Offerings shrink. Fewer names in books.

System isn't broken. It's stopping. Task by task.

[CH15 | 12:48–14:00 | 结尾回扣与主题对照句：用'读过与活过'的终极对照完成全片意义的统合，无CTA克制结束]

I don't have words for this. No inscription format allows it. No stela type lets you carve "the promise stopped." System records victories. No template for failure.

When you read about population decline, you see regional estimates. Across the southern Maya lowlands, estimates suggest a decline of more than 90 percent from peak to 950 CE, though the timing and scale varied by site.

When you live it? You walk past that altar every morning. Chisels untouched. Watch your assistant leave without goodbye.

When you read collapse, you see a date. When you live it, you pass the unfinished altar: one face carved, one begun, two left blank. The calendar turns, but the stonework has stopped.

issues.problem: 开头把“停工就是记录”的结论说得过早，也将无法证实的“并非延误”当成事实；改成问题，把解释留给后文。
issues.quote: This isn't just a delayed project. When your job is to maintain eternity—to mark time, to promise the gods that tomorrow will come like today came—a stone that stops being carved is a different kind of record. It's a record of stopping.
issues.fix: When your work is to mark time and keep the ceremonies going, an unfinished monument raises a question: what stopped?

issues.problem: 把身份和城市信息前置后，这里改为职责与日常经过场景；删除过长的身份解释，让开头更快进入画面。
issues.quote: I'm a Maya priest in 822 AD—ah k'in, the one who keeps the calendar, marks the ceremonies, watches the monuments. This is Copán, and I walk past this thing every single day.
issues.fix: It's 822 in Copán. As an ah k'in, I announce feast days and conduct local ceremonies. I pass this unfinished altar every day.

issues.problem: 原句没有说明工匠发生了什么；改为与“城市逐渐空去”的标题意象相连，同时不虚构他们离开的具体原因。
issues.quote: Waiting for hands that never came back.
issues.fix: Waiting for carvers who have left the city.

issues.problem: 删去与CH03重复的行动简报和“国王明知却不承认”的无证心理判断，保留前往王宫的任务线。
issues.quote: I need to go to the palace and find out why. I need to understand what happened to the carvers, what happened to the plan. And I need to tell the king something he probably already knows but won't admit: something has changed.
issues.fix: I need to reach the palace and tell the king what I can see: the carvers have left this work unfinished. I don't know what answer I'll get.

issues.problem: 把提纲式的“Public domain”并入口播句，并让重建素材和考古证据的关系更清楚。
issues.quote: Everything you're seeing is reconstructed from real artifacts—stone reliefs, murals, pottery. Public domain. AI adds color and environments, close as possible to archaeological evidence.
issues.fix: Everything you're seeing is reconstructed from public-domain Maya reliefs, murals, and pottery. AI adds color and settings, guided by the archaeological evidence.

issues.problem: “复杂十倍”没有可检验的衡量标准；改用两套历法的功能说明祭司职责。

issues.fix: One tracks sacred days; the other tracks the solar year. Your work is to calculate dates and announce the right ceremonies.

issues.problem: 原句把不同祭司职务及通行权限说得过于绝对；改成有限度的阶层对照，并补入等待这一具体摩擦。
issues.quote: The high priest walks straight into the palace. You? Send word through an attendant. Wait. Same knowledge, different doors.
issues.fix: A senior court priest can enter palace spaces more directly. You send word through an attendant and wait. The city gives different ranks different access.

issues.problem: 原稿用未经支持的“纸张减半”证明资源衰退；改为触觉细节，避免伪造历史数量。
issues.quote: You hand him tree bark paper for tonight's blood offering. Years ago, this stack would be twice as thick.
issues.fix: You hand him bark paper for tonight's offering. Its surface is smooth on one side and fibrous on the other; you feel the ridges as you turn it over.

issues.problem: 删除无依据的月份对比和具体仪式变化，把信息限定为主角听到的说法。
issues.quote: Last month, the high priest's ceremony had more. Now quietly cut. Nobody says why.
issues.fix: You have heard that offerings are being reduced. No one says why.

issues.problem: 把预告片式碎句改成自然完整的口播句。
issues.quote: Copal smoke thick. Your assistant sorting bundles—corn, twine.
issues.fix: Copal smoke hangs thick as your assistant sorts bundles of corn and twine.

issues.problem: 仪式动作不能证明所有参与者都持有相同信念；改为主角有限视角下的感受。
issues.quote: The whole plaza believes it. Certainty. Shared commitment.
issues.fix: You want to believe it too. For a moment, the shared ritual makes the promise feel real.

issues.problem: 提前建立资深祭司与主角的关系，避免关键配角在危机段突然出现。
issues.quote: When ceremony ends, a senior priest catches your eye. Tilts his head toward the edge, away from torches.
issues.fix: When the ceremony ends, the senior priest who taught you the calendar catches your eye and nods toward the edge of the plaza, away from the torches.

issues.problem: 没有证据证明特定国王曾作出这项承诺，也没有可确认的这段对话；改为神学背景与降雨状况的有限表述。
issues.quote: The rains. King promised. We bled. Gave offering. Rains didn't come.
issues.fix: The rites ask for rain. We made the offerings, and the rains have been poor.

issues.problem: 保留王宫材质反差，删除没有来源的庭院尺寸比较。
issues.quote: Jade inlay catches torchlight. Painted stucco—reds, blues, whites. Courtyard three times wider than your plaza.
issues.fix: Jade inlay catches the torchlight, and painted stucco carries reds, blues, and whites. The palace surfaces are more richly finished than the spaces you know at home.

issues.problem: 灰泥地板变薄是跨遗址考古观察，不能写成祭司当场发现或确定归因于缺木；改为说明证据范围与推断边界。
issues.quote: The floor. Top layer thinner than older sections. The elder said it three months ago—no trees left. Here, they're stretching what remains.
issues.fix: Archaeologists have found that plaster floors grew thinner over time at Maya sites. Making plaster required heavy fuel use, but that evidence cannot tell you what the palace workers here intended.

issues.problem: 强化宫廷与广场的资源反差，但不补造玉石运输、人力成本或其他未经核实的换算。
issues.quote: This beauty—and the plaza where attendance drops. Same city.
issues.fix: You feel the contrast sharply: this palace is still finished and bright, while the public work outside stands unfinished.

issues.problem: 删除事实材料未支持的出席者来源和身份名单，保留空间秩序体现等级的观察。
issues.quote: Nobles from allied cities, regional governors. Everyone knows where to stand. Seating geometry is a political map.
issues.fix: The nobles know where to stand. Their places mark rank.

issues.problem: 原稿对数量及其可供养家庭的时间作了无来源比较；保留供品类型，不夸大规模。
issues.quote: Offerings: copal resin, more than your temple burns in a month. Maize that could feed families for weeks.
issues.fix: The offerings include copal resin and maize, gathered for the ceremony.

issues.problem: 删除未经核实的祭坛陈设细节，保留王室空间与城镇祭司日常空间的区隔。
issues.quote: King's private altar behind carved screen. Quetzal feathers, obsidian mirrors.
issues.fix: The king's private altar sits behind a carved screen.

issues.problem: 把不清楚所指的“system”换成具体的资源集中与仪式延续。
issues.quote: Resources pulled from countryside, concentrated here. System still running.
issues.fix: Resources from across the city are concentrated here, and the ceremonies continue.

issues.problem: 修正与委托年代冲突的“两年”，用事实表支持的年份和祭坛状态取代虚构的倒计时。
issues.quote: February 822. Two years since king ordered that altar. Chisels haven't moved.
issues.fix: In 822, Ukit Took took the throne and commissioned the altar. One face was completed; work on the next stopped.

issues.problem: “全城只有主角看见”没有证据，且与其他祭司也察觉危机的情节矛盾；改成主角自己的理解。
issues.quote: You're the only one who walks past it daily. The only one who sees it as a timer.
issues.fix: You pass it every day, and you begin to read its unfinished faces as a measure of what has stopped.

issues.problem: 石碑纪年结束不等于城市逐个停止或变空；改为证据实际支持的表述。
issues.quote: One by one, stones stopped.
issues.fix: Across the region, the dated monument record ends at different times.

issues.problem: 让计划与CH12实际在仪式后遇见国王的情节不再冲突，并将对白保留为重建场景而非史料逐字记录。
issues.quote: Tomorrow morning, king holds ceremony at dawn. That's your window.
issues.fix: The king's ceremony is at dawn. If you are going to speak, it has to be before or during the rites.

issues.problem: 该回应属于神王制逻辑下的假设性重建，不是已知史料；缩短解释性话术，改为简洁宣告，不把卡顿周期应对说成确证引语。
issues.quote: We performed offerings. Bled for gods. Covenant doesn't break because one season is difficult. This is k'atun cycle. Next period restores balance.
issues.fix: The offerings are made. We have bled. The gods do not abandon those who honor them. This hard season will pass.

issues.problem: 原句中的“system”指代不清；改为说明王室回应的内容，并避免把它写成已记录的固定话术。
issues.quote: System has a script for this.
issues.fix: He answers with the assurance the court can offer: the rites have been performed, and order will return.

issues.problem: 删除抽象且重复的倒计时总结，让下一章承担时间和物证的推进。
issues.quote: You tried. But altar still unfinished. Countdown hasn't stopped.
issues.fix: You have said what you came to say. The altar is still unfinished.

issues.problem: 删除含混的“二月过去”，改用事实表可支持的年份和祭坛状态，避免制造月度倒计时。
issues.quote: 822. February passed. Altar still there. One face done, second begun, two blank. Chisels unmoved.
issues.fix: In 822, the altar remains unfinished: one face complete, a second begun, and two blank. The chisels remain where the work stopped.

issues.problem: 原句把区域性人口迁移写成主角在该时点亲眼所见；给定事实只支持区域迁徙趋势，不支持这个现场场景。

edits.old: This isn't just a delayed project. When your job is to maintain eternity—to mark time, to promise the gods that tomorrow will come like today came—a stone that stops being carved is a different kind of record. It's a record of stopping.
edits.new: When your work is to mark time and keep the ceremonies going, an unfinished monument raises a question: what stopped?
edits.reason: 开头把“停工就是记录”的结论说得过早，也将无法证实的“并非延误”当成事实；改成问题，把解释留给后文。

edits.old: I'm a Maya priest in 822 AD—ah k'in, the one who keeps the calendar, marks the ceremonies, watches the monuments. This is Copán, and I walk past this thing every single day.
edits.new: It's 822 in Copán. As an ah k'in, I announce feast days and conduct local ceremonies. I pass this unfinished altar every day.
edits.reason: 把身份和城市信息前置后，这里改为职责与日常经过场景；删除过长的身份解释，让开头更快进入画面。

edits.old: Waiting for hands that never came back.
edits.new: Waiting for carvers who have left the city.
edits.reason: 原句没有说明工匠发生了什么；改为与“城市逐渐空去”的标题意象相连，同时不虚构他们离开的具体原因。

edits.old: I need to go to the palace and find out why. I need to understand what happened to the carvers, what happened to the plan. And I need to tell the king something he probably already knows but won't admit: something has changed.
edits.new: I need to reach the palace and tell the king what I can see: the carvers have left this work unfinished. I don't know what answer I'll get.
edits.reason: 删去与CH03重复的行动简报和“国王明知却不承认”的无证心理判断，保留前往王宫的任务线。

edits.new: Everything you're seeing is reconstructed from public-domain Maya reliefs, murals, and pottery. AI adds color and settings, guided by the archaeological evidence.
edits.reason: 把提纲式的“Public domain”并入口播句，并让重建素材和考古证据的关系更清楚。

edits.old: Two tasks: see the palace zones. Find the king, tell him.
edits.reason: 这项任务已在CH01交代，重复出现没有带来新信息。

edits.old: Will they listen? Let's start with your daily work.
edits.new: Your day begins with the calendar.

edits.old: Ten times more complex than a lunar calendar. Your job: keep them turning.
edits.new: One tracks sacred days; the other tracks the solar year. Your work is to calculate dates and announce the right ceremonies.
edits.reason: “复杂十倍”没有可检验的衡量标准；改用两套历法的功能说明祭司职责。

edits.old: The high priest walks straight into the palace. You? Send word through an attendant. Wait. Same knowledge, different doors.
edits.new: A senior court priest can enter palace spaces more directly. You send word through an attendant and wait. The city gives different ranks different access.
edits.reason: 原句把不同祭司职务及通行权限说得过于绝对；改成有限度的阶层对照，并补入等待这一具体摩擦。

edits.old: You hand him tree bark paper for tonight's blood offering. Years ago, this stack would be twice as thick.
edits.new: You hand him bark paper for tonight's offering. Its surface is smooth on one side and fibrous on the other; you feel the ridges as you turn it over.
edits.reason: 原稿用未经支持的“纸张减半”证明资源衰退；改为触觉细节，避免伪造历史数量。

edits.old: Last month, the high priest's ceremony had more. Now quietly cut. Nobody says why.
edits.new: You have heard that offerings are being reduced. No one says why.
edits.reason: 删除无依据的月份对比和具体仪式变化，把信息限定为主角听到的说法。

edits.old: Copal smoke thick. Your assistant sorting bundles—corn, twine.
edits.new: Copal smoke hangs thick as your assistant sorts bundles of corn and twine.

edits.old: The whole plaza believes it. Certainty. Shared commitment.
edits.new: You want to believe it too. For a moment, the shared ritual makes the promise feel real.

edits.new: When the ceremony ends, the senior priest who taught you the calendar catches your eye and nods toward the edge of the plaza, away from the torches.
edits.reason: 提前建立资深祭司与主角的关系，避免关键配角在危机段突然出现。

[CH01 | 0:00–0:36 | 沉浸式开场：第一秒落地时空身位，挂出两条任务线，建立第一人称在场框架]

This is a stone altar. It was supposed to have four carved sides showing the king's glory. It has one. The chisels are still sitting there. No one has touched them in two years.

I'm a Maya priest in 822 AD—ah k'in, the one who keeps the calendar, marks the ceremonies, watches the monuments. This is Copán, and I walk past this thing every single day.

Here's what I know: the king ordered this altar carved two years ago. One side finished—the king's coronation scene, perfect detail. The second side? Started and stopped. Two sides completely blank. And those chisels. Still right there. Waiting for hands that never came back.

This isn't just a delayed project. When your job is to maintain eternity—to mark time, to promise the gods that tomorrow will come like today came—a stone that stops being carved is a different kind of record. It's a record of stopping.

I need to go to the palace and find out why. I need to understand what happened to the carvers, what happened to the plan. And I need to tell the king something he probably already knows but won't admit: something has changed.

[CH02 | 0:36–1:12 | 真实性契约与制作说明：声明素材来源、复原方法、时代标注，建立观众对'所见即所考'的信任]

Everything you're seeing is reconstructed from real artifacts—stone reliefs, murals, pottery. Public domain. AI adds color and environments, close as possible to archaeological evidence.

One complication: some ritual details come from 16th century records, 600 years later. I'll tell you when we're bridging that gap.

[CH03 | 1:12–1:48 | 任务简报与探索清单：列出祭司的两条行动线，同时暗示中点的两个对比性结局]

As town priest—ah k'in—you announce feast days, conduct rituals, oversee monument carving.

You've noticed things. Carvers say no lime, trees gone. Ceremony crowds half. Rains didn't come.

Two tasks: see the palace zones. Find the king, tell him.

Will they listen? Let's start with your daily work.

[CH04 | 1:48–3:08 | 进入神庙区的阶层检查与日常生活流：用感官细节与现代参照系建立'活人感'，同时展示权力等级制度]

Temple precinct. Copal incense thick in your throat. Your desk: stone carved with calendar wheels. Tree-bark paper, red and black ink. You copy tribute lists, check feast days.

Two calendars run at once. 260-day Tzolk'in, sacred calendar. 365-day Haab'—eighteen months of twenty days, plus five unlucky days. They mesh like gears. Every 52 years they return to the same point. One Calendar Round.

Ten times more complex than a lunar calendar. Your job: keep them turning.

The high priest walks straight into the palace. You? Send word through an attendant. Wait. Same knowledge, different doors.

Today: preparing for year-bearer ceremony. Confirm date, arrange offerings.

Your job is keeping these wheels from failing. They're already failing. No one with direct access notices.

[CH05 | 3:08–4:20 | 与同事/助手的对话与仪式供品清单：用配角的小梦想人化遇难者，预告当晚活动，同时暗示资源消耗]

Copal smoke thick. Your assistant sorting bundles—corn, twine.

"After this season, maybe I ask for my own posting. Town priest somewhere smaller. My son's learning glyphs."

He says it like the path is already there.

You hand him tree bark paper for tonight's blood offering. Years ago, this stack would be twice as thick.

"Offerings ready. Copal. Corn. Two chickens."

Last month, the high priest's ceremony had more. Now quietly cut. Nobody says why.

"We should change into ceremonial garments soon."

He looks at you like he wants to ask something. Doesn't.

"Will you see the new stela I carved?" His first major work. "Not like the masters did twenty years ago, but... what I could manage."

You promise you will.

[CH06 | 4:20–5:34 | 集体仪式高光与小型社群时刻：用归属感与共同体验制造情绪高峰，为后段的崩解蓄能]

That night, ceremony in the plaza. Year-bearer ritual. City gathers.

Torches. Drums echo off pyramid steps. Copal smoke. Heat of bodies swaying in rhythm.

Nobles first. Stingray spines, obsidian blades—piercing tongues, blood dripping onto bark paper. Some do it publicly here. Paper soaks dark red, gets burned in braziers.

Then commoners. Most pierce earlobes. A few do tongues. Everyone bleeds.

Someone says it: "This is our promise. We bleed, they send rain."

The whole plaza believes it. Certainty. Shared commitment.

When ceremony ends, a senior priest catches your eye. Tilts his head toward the edge, away from torches.

You follow into shadows. He waits until drumming fades.

[CH07 | 5:34–6:56 | 内部知情者的坦白与危机确认：用私密对话完成'元设定溶解'，锁定观众对危机迹象的第一次完整认知]

"Stone carvers," he says. "They told you about the trees?"

You nod.

"Told me three months ago. No trees close enough. Can't burn lime."

"Last month's ceremony. Maybe forty people. A year ago? Hundreds."

He doesn't look surprised.

"The rains. King promised. We bled. Gave offering. Rains didn't come."

You both stand there. The contract is supposed to work. King bleeds, gods send rain.

"Tomorrow. King holds ceremony at dawn. Palace compound. That's the window."

He walks back. You're not the only one who sees it. Tomorrow you'll go.

[CH08 | 6:56–8:00 | 进入王宫礼仪区的禁入奇观：用阶层对比与材质细节制造视觉冲击，同时加深任务的紧迫感]

You enter the palace ceremonial zone—assisting with ritual preparations.

Jade inlay catches torchlight. Painted stucco—reds, blues, whites. Courtyard three times wider than your plaza.

The floor. Top layer thinner than older sections. The elder said it three months ago—no trees left. Here, they're stretching what remains.

Nobles pass without looking. You stay near edges.

Lords discussing tomorrow's ceremony step over that thinning floor like it's eternal.

This beauty—and the plaza where attendance drops. Same city.

[CH09 | 8:00–8:54 | 王室仪式的盛宴与消费规模目录：用数字与专属性把繁荣推到顶点，为后段的倒计时蓄势]

They're performing permanence.

Tomorrow, katun ceremony—twenty-year cycle renewal. Lords gathering.

Nobles from allied cities, regional governors. Everyone knows where to stand. Seating geometry is a political map.

Offerings: copal resin, more than your temple burns in a month. Maize that could feed families for weeks.

No one seems surprised. This is normal. Always has been.

High priest's study. Walls painted with gods from underworld. Fire bowls jade-rimmed. This is where the calendar is kept.

King's private altar behind carved screen. Quetzal feathers, obsidian mirrors.

Resources pulled from countryside, concentrated here. System still running.

But you remember simplified offerings in the plaza. What the carver said about wood. Not sustainable.

[CH10 | 8:54–9:36 | 调性切换与倒计时开启：点名确切日期，从探索模式切换为宿命模式，所有幽默节拍归零]

You stand on pyramid. City below.

February 822. Two years since king ordered that altar. Chisels haven't moved.

You're the only one who walks past it daily. The only one who sees it as a timer.

Palenque: 799. Yaxchilán: 808. Copán: 822. Tikal: 889. Toniná: 909.

One by one, stones stopped.

People below still believing next katun restores everything.

[CH11 | 9:36–10:36 | 干预计划的彩排与准备：交代所有的情报、机会、说辞与时间限制，让观众与主角一起预演失败]

Tomorrow morning, king holds ceremony at dawn. That's your window.

You rehearse.

"Lord, three things. No wood for lime. Ritual attendance half. Rains you promised—they haven't come."

You know what he'll say. "We performed the rites. Gods do not abandon those who honor them."

Phrases designed to end doubt.

You pack incense pouch. Check calendar scroll.

Someone has to say it.

[CH12 | 10:36–11:12 | 警告被驳回与使命收束：向权力说真话，却得到了克制的拒绝，观众与主角一起体验无力感与和解]

You find him after ritual. Corridor between throne room and altar.

"My lord. No wood for lime. Attendance half. Rains you promised haven't come."

He listens. Then speaks, calm.

"We performed offerings. Bled for gods. Covenant doesn't break because one season is difficult. This is k'atun cycle. Next period restores balance."

System has a script for this.

You tried. But altar still unfinished. Countdown hasn't stopped.

[CH13 | 11:12–12:00 | 倒计时的物理撞击与见证者的独白：时间戳报时、知情独白、目击瞬间、旁观者毫无所觉的对比]

822. February passed. Altar still there. One face done, second begun, two blank. Chisels unmoved.

You walk past daily. Most don't look anymore.

Carvers didn't return. Not February. Not March. Not after.

Up north, people leaving. Quietly. Moving toward Yucatan.

Market stalls empty. Harvest fields short.

Someone says, "Perhaps next rainy season." As if this is pause, not stop.

You're the only one who knows no new stelae are being carved.

[CH14 | 12:00–12:48 | 官方措辞与真相的落差、数字对比与拒绝面对现实的细节：见证者情绪决堤与崩解独白]

They're still saying it's temporary.

But bones don't agree. Burials show growth lines stopped, teeth underdeveloped, adults shorter. Chronic starvation in skeleton.

Plaza rituals? Attendance dropped to half what it was five years ago. Hundreds used to come. Now fifty.

They repeat what the king said—as if next cycle fixes this.

As ah k'in, my duty is to maintain these cycles. But every dawn I announce festival dates, fewer listen. Offerings shrink. Fewer names in books.

System isn't broken. It's stopping. Task by task.

[CH15 | 12:48–14:00 | 结尾回扣与主题对照句：用'读过与活过'的终极对照完成全片意义的统合，无CTA克制结束]

I don't have words for this. No inscription format allows it. No stela type lets you carve "the promise stopped." System records victories. No template for failure.

When you read Maya collapse, it's a date. "Southern Lowlands population declined over 90%." One line.

When you live it? You walk past that altar every morning. Chisels untouched. Watch your assistant leave without goodbye.

Like those stelae—Palenque, Yaxchilán, Copán, one by one they stopped. Sometimes, the truest history is what they left blank.

That unfinished altar? The most honest monument Copán ever built.

When you read collapse, you see a number. When you live collapse, you see the empty seat. The work continues. Calendar turns. No one reads it.

factcheck.overview:
### 1. 风险总览

共 20 条待核问题：4 条高风险、13 条中风险、3 条低风险；没有显式计算题，但藏着 4 处日期减法。

最严重（高）：CH01「the king ordered this altar carved two years ago」＋CH10「February 822. Two years ago, king carved the first altar side」与 F01/F23 冲突——L 祭坛的委托者是 Ukit Took，他 822 年 2 月 6/10 日才登基，第一面刻的就是他的登基场景，不可能在 820 年由他下令。这条既是开篇钩子的支点，也是全片倒计时装置的支点，一旦被懂行观众抓住，开头 30 秒塌方。

次严重（高）：CH05 的供品清单「Two chickens」——鸡是旧大陆家禽，16 世纪才随西班牙人进入美洲，前哥伦布供品应为火鸡。它藏在最具沉浸感的细节里，最容易被识破。

高：仪式观众数字（CH07「forty / a year ago hundreds」、CH14「fifty / five years ago hundreds」、CH15「twelve」）没有任何史前数据来源（F33 本身就标[假设]），且三处基线互相矛盾，而这正是"观众变少"这条核心论点的唯一量化支撑，属论点最脆弱环节。

中风险集中在：卡顿算术（「Twenty years away」）、CH02 承诺标注 16 世纪尤卡坦材料却在 CH04/CH06/CH09 一次也没标、卡顿大典与"标准放血仪式"前后矛盾、「Every major city」绝对化、灰泥地板「Half an inch」具体值、90% 口径从佩滕核心区放大到整个南部低地、"无任何铭文记录崩溃"依赖[待查]来源。低风险两条为 ah k'in 职掌合并与树皮纸存量描述。国王拒绝的台词（F32[假设]）写成引语，需标注为重建。

### 2. 计算依赖链

1. 822 − 2 = 820 → 祭坛开工年 → 决定 CH01 钩子「两年没人碰」、CH10 报时、CH13「车床仍未动」、CH15 收束。若委托年＝822（F01），整条"两年"依赖链作废：要么把开工年改成 822 年当年、把"two years"改成"since the accession"，要么把场景后移到 824 年并让国王仍是 Ukit Took。
2. 观众数：CH07 40 人／"一年前数百" → CH14 50 人／"五年前数百＝half" → CH15 12 人。三处推不出同一个"减半"结论：40 与 50 差 25%，"a year ago"与"five years ago"是两个基线，"twelve"又不等于 50 的一半。任一处改数，CH07/CH14/CH15 三条句子要一起改。
3. 822 所在卡顿为 9.19（810–830），下一次卡顿结束在 830 年，距 822 约 8 年 → CH13「Twenty years away」多算 12 年；这句话支撑"把希望推到下一代、结果谁也等不到"的收束结论。
4. 1566 − 822 = 744 年（对 900 年则是 666 年）→ CH02「600 years later」少算约 60–140 年。
5. 90%（佩滕核心区，F18）→ CH15 扩大为「Southern Lowlands」，口径放大；若观众按整个南部低地核对，数字对不上。

木材短缺导致的石灰无法烧制，进而无法继续雕刻
仪式参加人数大幅下降，从数百人降到五十人左右
各主要城市的石碑雕刻先后停止（帕伦克799年、亚克奇兰808年、科潘822年、提卡尔889年、托尼纳909年）
应许的雨季没有来临
祭司的日常职责：维持两套历法的运转（260天的Tzolk'in和365天的Haab'），宣布庆典日期，监督纪念碑雕刻
宫殿地板变薄（比老地板少半英寸），表明石灰燃料紧张导致质量下降
人口迁移，人们默默离开，向尤卡坦半岛移动以寻找水源
骨骼证据显示长期营养不良（生长线停止、牙齿发育不全、成人身材矮小）
祭司向国王说出三个事实但被以官方措辞驳回，国王声称这是k'atun周期的波动，下一个周期会恢复平衡

problems.quote_zh: 你知道这意味着什么。每平方米要烧二十棵树。燃料快没了。他们在缩水。
problems.problem: 信息双重总结:CH07已经让祭司说出「三个月前就知道没有树了」，CH08开头的宫殿地板段落重新讲了一遍同一个结论（燃料不足）。这两个地方都在讲「木材短缺→石灰问题」这个因果链。
problems.fix: CH08保留宫殿地板的细节观察（厚度变薄的视觉冲击），但把「燃料快没了」这一句改成一句回顾，比如改成「正如那位长老三个月前说的，树都没了」，然后直接进入「这种美和广场参加人数下降在同一座城市」这个新对比。。观点、论点本身不能删:第一次讲透的地方不动,只把这一处重复的几句压成一句回顾,接着讲这一章本来的新内容;压掉的字数用这一章已有内容的细节补(场景、算账过程),不加新事实、新数字、新观点,不要让篇幅变短;不改任何数字,不动章节结构和别的句子。

problems.quote_zh: 我无法继续假装。每天黎明我宣布庆典日期、标记历法周期。

problems.fix: 在「Every dawn I announce」前加一句，比如「作为ah k'in，我的工作就是宣布这些日期、维持这些周期」或「作为保守历法的人」，一句话把职责拎出来，然后继续「Every dawn」的新感悟。。观点、论点本身不能删:第一次讲透的地方不动,只把这一处重复的几句压成一句回顾,接着讲这一章本来的新内容;压掉的字数用这一章已有内容的细节补(场景、算账过程),不加新事实、新数字、新观点,不要让篇幅变短;不改任何数字,不动章节结构和别的句子。

problems.quote: Sometimes, the truest history is what they left blank.
problems.quote_zh: 有时候，最真实的历史是他们留下的空白。
problems.problem: 信息缺回顾:CH10讲透了各城市石碑先后停止雕刻的时间表（帕伦克799、亚克奇兰808、科潘822等），到CH15的最后已经隔了四分多钟。在结尾「Sometimes, the truest history is what they left blank」这一句用了这个观点（未完成的东西记录真相），但完全没有提醒观众这是指CH10的那个石碑停止清单。观众容易以为这是结尾的抒情总结，忘了背后指的是具体的历史事实。

history.text:
This is a stone altar. It was supposed to have four carved sides showing the king's glory. It has one. The chisels are still sitting there. No one has touched them in two years.

I'm a Maya priest in 822 AD—ah k'in, the one who keeps the calendar, marks the ceremonies, watches the monuments. This is Copán, and I walk past this thing every single day.

Here's what I know: the king ordered this altar carved two years ago. One side finished—the king's coronation scene, perfect detail. The second side? Started and stopped. Two sides completely blank. And those chisels. Still right there. Waiting for hands that never came back.

This isn't just a delayed project. When your job is to maintain eternity—to mark time, to promise the gods that tomorrow will come like today came—a stone that stops being carved is a different kind of record. It's a record of stopping.

I need to go to the palace and find out why. I need to understand what happened to the carvers, what happened to the plan. And I need to tell the king something he probably already knows but won't admit: something has changed.

Everything you're seeing is reconstructed from real artifacts—stone reliefs, murals, pottery. Public domain. AI adds color and builds environments, close as possible to archaeological evidence.

One complication: some ritual details come from 1560s records, 600 years later. I'll tell you when we're bridging that gap.

What does a priest do daily? What tasks can stop?

"Stone carvers," he says. "They told you about the trees?"

You nod.

"Told me the same three months ago. No trees close enough. Can't burn lime without fuel. That altar—"

"Not just trees," you say. "Last month's ceremony. Maybe forty people. A year ago? Hundreds."

He doesn't look surprised. Just tired.

"The rains. King promised. We performed the bloodletting. Gave the offering. Year turned over. Rains didn't come."

You both stand there. The contract is supposed to work. King bleeds, gods send rain, maize grows. That's how time continues.

"Tomorrow. King holds ceremony at dawn. Palace compound. If you're going to say something, that's the window."

He meets your eyes. Nods once. Walks back.

You stand in the dark. You're not the only one who sees it. But knowing together doesn't make it lighter.

Tomorrow you'll go to the palace.

You enter the palace ceremonial zone—assisting with ritual preparations.

Everything changes.

Jade inlay catches torchlight. Painted stucco—reds, blues, whites—dense patterns everywhere. Courtyard three times wider than your plaza.

You look down. The floor. Early temple floors had limestone slabs over a foot thick. Here, the top layer is thinner than it should be. Half an inch less than older sections.

You know what that means. Each square meter burns twenty trees. Fuel's running low. They're stretching it thinner.

Nobles pass without looking. You stay near edges. Learn where to stand, where to avert eyes.

Lords walk by discussing tomorrow's ceremony. They step over that thinning floor like it's eternal.

This beauty—and the plaza where attendance drops. Same city. Luxury still here, burning through what's left.

You stand on the pyramid. City spreads below.

February 822. Two years ago, king carved the first altar side. Work was supposed to accelerate. Second face should be halfway done. Third and fourth still blank.

Chisels haven't moved in two years.

You're the only one who walks past that stone every day. The only one who sees it as a timer.

Palenque: last stone, 799. Yaxchilán: 808. You: 822. Tikal: 889. Toniná: 909.

Every major city. One by one, stones stopped.

This isn't delay. This is the record ending.

People below still waiting. Still believing the next katun will restore everything.

You decide.

Tomorrow morning, king holds ceremony at dawn. Standard bloodletting. That's your window.

You know the rhythm. King arrives first light, performs offering. Between bloodletting and final blessing, people approach with reports. You're ah k'in. You have standing.

You rehearse.

"Lord, three things. Stonemasons say no wood left for lime. Ritual attendance last month—half expected. Rains you promised. They haven't come."

You try different openings. Settle on direct. Facts, not interpretations.

But you know what he'll say. "We performed the rites. Gave blood. Gods do not abandon those who honor them." Or: "This is katun cycle oscillation. Next turn brings abundance."

Phrases designed to end doubt.

You find him after ritual. Corridor between throne room and private altar. He's removing ceremonial headband.

"My lord. Three things. No more wood for lime. Ritual attendance half what it was. Rains you promised. They haven't come."

He listens. Then speaks, voice calm.

"We performed the offerings. Bled for the gods. Covenant does not break because one season is difficult. This is k'atun cycle. It turns. Next period restores balance."

An answer so complete it leaves no room for reply. System has a script for this. Inscriptions don't record doubts.

You tried.

But the altar is still unfinished. Chisels still there. Countdown hasn't stopped.

822. February passed. Altar still there.

One face shows king's accession. Second begun. Two blank. Chisels haven't moved.

You walk past it every day. Most don't look anymore.

Carvers didn't come back. Not in February. Not March. Not after. In other cities, same thing. Up north, people leaving. Quietly. Moving toward Yucatan, where water doesn't fail.

Fewer people at market. Fewer hands for harvest.

Someone says, "Perhaps next rainy season will be better." As if this is a pause, not a stop.

"Perhaps next katun." Twenty years away.

But you're the only one who knows no new stelae are being carved.

Chisels still there.

822. February passed. Altar still there. One face done, second begun, two blank. Chisels unmoved.

Carvers didn't return. Not February. Not March. Not after.

Market stalls empty. Harvest fields short.

Someone says, "Perhaps next rainy season." As if this is pause, not stop.

You're the only one who knows no new stelae are being carved.

They're still saying it's temporary.

But bones don't agree. Burials show growth lines stopped partway, teeth underdeveloped, adults shorter. Chronic starvation written into skeleton.

Royal ceremonies keep happening. But plaza rituals? Attendance dropped to half what it was five years ago. Hundreds used to come. Now fifty, half look like they have to be there.

"Rains will return next cycle." They believe it. They have to.

I can't keep pretending. Every dawn I announce festival dates, mark calendar cycles. Every time fewer listen. Offerings get smaller. Fewer names in tally books.

System isn't broken. It's just stopping. Task by task.

They're still saying it's temporary.

But bones don't agree. Burials show growth lines stopped, teeth underdeveloped, adults shorter. Chronic starvation in skeleton.

Plaza rituals? Attendance dropped to half what it was five years ago. Hundreds used to come. Now fifty.

They repeat what the king said—as if next cycle fixes this.

As ah k'in, my duty is to maintain these cycles. But every dawn I announce festival dates, fewer listen. Offerings shrink. Fewer names in books.

System isn't broken. It's stopping. Task by task.

I don't have the words. No inscription format for this. No stela type that lets you carve "the promise stopped working." System was built to announce victories—permanence carved into stone. No template for failure. So it doesn't get written.

When you read about Maya collapse, it's a date. A footnote: "Southern Lowlands population declined over 90%." One line.

But when you live it? You walk past that altar every morning. See chisels untouched. Watch your assistant leave without goodbye. Keep announcing ceremony dates to empty plaza. Write tallies no one collects. Keep calibrating sacred calendar—knowing fewer show up, knowing rain hasn't come, knowing that stone will never be finished.

People who wrote inscriptions only recorded what kings wanted remembered. Kings don't commission stelae saying "we failed." So silence becomes the record. That unfinished altar? That's the most honest monument Copán ever built.

When you read collapse, you see a number. When you live collapse, you see the empty seat. Supply list getting shorter. Plaza that held hundreds now holds twelve. Children with bones too thin. Families who left without telling anyone.

History gets written by people with chisels and the right to carve. Sometimes, the truest history is what they left blank.

I don't have words for this. No inscription format allows it. No stela type lets you carve "the promise stopped." System records victories. No template for failure.

When you read Maya collapse, it's a date. "Southern Lowlands population declined over 90%." One line.

When you live it? You walk past that altar every morning. Chisels untouched. Watch your assistant leave without goodbye.

Like those stelae—Palenque, Yaxchilán, Copán, one by one they stopped. Sometimes, the truest history is what they left blank.

That unfinished altar? The most honest monument Copán ever built.

When you read collapse, you see a number. When you live collapse, you see the empty seat. The work continues. Calendar turns. No one reads it.

As town priest—ah k'in—you announce feast days, conduct rituals, oversee monument carving.

You've noticed things. Carvers say no lime, trees gone. Ceremony crowds half. Rains didn't come.

Two tasks: see the palace zones. Find the king, tell him.

Will they listen? Let's start with your daily work.

Temple precinct. Copal incense thick in your throat. Your desk: stone carved with calendar wheels. Tree-bark paper, red and black ink. You copy tribute lists, check feast days.

Two calendars run at once. 260-day Tzolk'in, sacred calendar. 365-day Haab'—eighteen months of twenty days, plus five unlucky days. They mesh like gears. Every 52 years they return to the same point. One Calendar Round.

Ten times more complex than a lunar calendar. Your job: keep them turning.

The high priest walks straight into the palace. You? Send word through an attendant. Wait. Same knowledge, different doors.

Today: preparing for year-bearer ceremony. Confirm date, arrange offerings.

Your job is keeping these wheels from failing. They're already failing. No one with direct access notices.

Copal smoke thick. Your assistant sorting bundles—corn, twine.

"After this season, maybe I ask for my own posting. Town priest somewhere smaller. My son's learning glyphs."

He says it like the path is already there.

You hand him tree bark paper for tonight's blood offering. Years ago, this stack would be twice as thick.

"Offerings ready. Copal. Corn. Two chickens."

Last month, the high priest's ceremony had more. Now quietly cut. Nobody says why.

"We should change into ceremonial garments soon."

He looks at you like he wants to ask something. Doesn't.

"Will you see the new stela I carved?" His first major work. "Not like the masters did twenty years ago, but... what I could manage."

You promise you will.

That night, ceremony in the plaza. Year-bearer ritual. City gathers.

Torches. Drums echo off pyramid steps. Copal smoke. Heat of bodies swaying in rhythm.

Nobles first. Stingray spines, obsidian blades—piercing tongues, blood dripping onto bark paper. Some do it publicly here. Paper soaks dark red, gets burned in braziers.

Then commoners. Most pierce earlobes. A few do tongues. Everyone bleeds.

Someone says it: "This is our promise. We bleed, they send rain."

The whole plaza believes it. Certainty. Shared commitment.

When ceremony ends, a senior priest catches your eye. Tilts his head toward the edge, away from torches.

You follow into shadows. He waits until drumming fades.

They're performing permanence.

Tomorrow, katun ceremony—twenty-year cycle renewal. Lords gathering.

Nobles from allied cities, regional governors. Everyone knows where to stand. Seating geometry is a political map.

Offerings: copal resin, more than your temple burns in a month. Maize that could feed families for weeks.

No one seems surprised. This is normal. Always has been.

High priest's study. Walls painted with gods from underworld. Fire bowls jade-rimmed. This is where the calendar is kept.

King's private altar behind carved screen. Quetzal feathers, obsidian mirrors.

Resources pulled from countryside, concentrated here. System still running.

But you remember simplified offerings in the plaza. What the carver said about wood. Not sustainable.

opening.hook: 用一座刻了一半就没人碰的祭坛，把观众直接放进一个每天路过它的祭司视角里，逼出「为什么停了」的疑问。
strengths: 第1–5句：前5秒用一个具体物件（祭坛）加两个相互矛盾的细节（本应四面、只刻一面；凿子在那、没人碰）把冲突立住，不靠旁白解释，观众自己看见反差。
第6–7句：身份交代干净，ah k'in 这个玛雅语词增加真实感，同时把「每天路过」做成一个持续压力，暗示后面会有更多发现。
第16–18句：用「这不只是一个被耽误的工程」做转折，把物件升格成论点切入口，给出本片核心问题的第一个甜头——停止本身是一种记录——节奏恰好在45秒前落地，符合蓝图要求。
第9–15句：把「一面完成、第二面停、两面空白、凿子还在」拆成短促的碎句，制造视觉扫描感，让观众跟着祭司的眼睛一格一格看祭坛，停顿感强。
risks: 第6句（0:14）：句子里同时出现「822 AD」和「ah k'in」两个需要接收的新信息，加上破折号和从句，密度偏高；口播时听众跟不上可能直接划走。改法：把 ah k'in 的解释拆到下一句，这句只说「我是公元822年的玛雅祭司」，简洁收住。
第5句（0:10）：「two years」是本片第二个数字，前10秒已经出现「four」（第2句），共两个数字，刚好踩在硬规则上限（最多1个）。违反硬规则，必须改。改法：删掉第2句里的「four」，改成「本来应该四面都刻满浮雕」换成「本来应该刻满国王荣耀」，把 four 去掉，前10秒只保留 two years 这一个数字。
第10–15句：把祭坛状态拆成六个极短句，口播里单句停顿过密，连续出现可能让节奏碎掉显得刻意。改法：把第10–12句合并成一句「第二面才开了个头，剩下两面完全空着」，减少停顿次数。
第17句（0:46）：这句是全段最长的句子，一口气塞了「记录时间、许诺神灵、明天如今天」三个并列概念，口播听一遍难以消化。改法：删掉「to promise the gods that tomorrow will come like today came」这个从句，保留「当你的职责是维持永恒——记录时间、主持仪式——」即可，意思不丢，句子短一半。
fix_plain: 第2句把「four carved sides」里的「four」删掉，改成「It was supposed to have carved sides showing the king's glory」，前10秒只保留第5句的「two years」一个数字，否则违反硬规则。
第6句拆成两句：先说「我是公元822年的玛雅祭司」收住，再另起一句说「ah k'in——负责守历法、主持仪式的那种」，避免一句话塞太多新词。
第10–12句合并成一句「第二面才起了个头，剩下两面完全空着」，减少连续短句停顿，口播更顺。
第17句删掉「to promise the gods that tomorrow will come like today came」这段，保留「当你的职责是维持永恒——记录时间、主持仪式」即可，句子减半，口播不掉人。
opening.score_why: 前30秒：第1–7句在8秒内给出人物和场景，标题冲突在14秒出现，物件与反差立住，但第5句和第2句共用了两个数字（four、two years），违反前10秒最多1个数字的硬规则，扣分；30–60秒：第16–18句在44秒给出第一个甜头「停止本身是一种记录」，悬念方向清晰，但第17句过长、信息密度过高，口播衔接有掉人风险，整体完成度高于平均但略逊于原片节奏的干净程度。

audit.report:
# YouTube文案逆向工程审稿报告

## 一、赛道与内容类型识别

### 参考视频
- **内容赛道**: 历史沉浸体验内容
- **内容类型**: 第一人称历史沉浸vlog + 戏剧反讽叙事
- **主要形式**: 故事叙述、历史重现、情绪共鸣、见证者视角
- **核心机制**: 已知结局 + 第一人称在场 + 探索禁区 + 注定失败的警告 + 轻→重调性切换

### 新视频
- **内容赛道**: 历史沉浸体验内容
- **内容类型**: 第一人称历史见证 + 文明崩溃纪实
- **主要形式**: 故事叙述、考古复原、渐进式崩解见证
- **核心机制**: 缓慢倒计时 + 祭司视角 + 日常任务失效 + 永恒承诺破裂

### 赛道关系
**同赛道迁移**。两者都使用第一人称沉浸式历史体验框架,观众与主角对结局的信息差构成核心张力。

### 本类内容的关键质量标准
1. **第一人称视角一致性**: 全程维持"我是祭司"的身份设定,不跳出
2. **历史细节可信度**: 考据细节的密度与准确性,建立"所见即所考"的信任
3. **戏剧反讽张力**: 观众知道玛雅崩溃,主角在场但无力阻止的张力管理
4. **调性切换完成度**: 从日常探索的轻快到倒计时的沉重,切换必须明确且不可逆
5. **情绪曲线管理**: 前段归属感 → 中段紧张 → 后段崩解的递进完整性
6. **见证者情感真实性**: 最后崩解段落是否有足够具体的场景支撑情绪

---

## 二、评分标准与总体结论

### 评分明细表

| 评分维度 | 权重 | 实际得分 | 扣分原因 |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| 标题与内容兑现 | 8 | 6 | 标题"Cities Empty"(复数)承诺多座城市,但文案90%聚焦科潘一地一座祭坛;F02列举的五城时间线(帕伦克799-托尼那909)在FS10一笔带过,未形成"城市逐个熄灭"的视觉化递进 |

| 结尾主题收束 | 7 | 6 | CH15主题对照句("When you read...when you live...")成立,但**意象回收不够具体**——原片结尾有"gasps"与音乐淡出的明确指示,新版"That unfinished altar? The most honest monument Copán ever built"是好句,但缺少最后一个画面定格(如"我又一次走过那块祭坛,凿子还在那里,上面落了两年的灰尘") |

### 总分与质量水平

**总分: 76/100**

**质量水平**: 良好,但尚未达到可发布标准

**三大优势**:
1. **开场祭坛意象强**: CH01用L祭坛的未完成状态作为全片隐喻,具象且有力
2. **双任务线结构清晰**: 探索王宫+警告国王两条线索明确,框架迁移核心成立
3. **主题论点站得住**: "读过vs活过""崩溃是每天发生"的论点有新意且有事实支撑

**三大致命问题**:
1. **倒计时压迫感缺失**(影响戏剧反讽核心): FS11-FS14应是全片张力峰值,但820-822两年间的"每一天"未被视觉化,直接跳到终点削弱了"缓慢崩溃"的主题承诺
2. **情绪峰值段落无支撑**(影响观众留存): FS07归属感、FS15崩解两处关键情绪点缺乏具体场景,只有抽象描写,无法让观众共情
3. **标题承诺未兑现**(影响点击-内容匹配): "Cities Empty"(复数)未在内容中体现,F02五城时间线被浪费

**当前是否适合发布**: **否**。核心问题(倒计时压迫感、情绪支撑、标题兑现)直接影响观众留存与主题完整性,必须修复后再发布。

## 四、逐段诊断——具体问题定位

### 问题编号:P01

**原文位置**: CH10-CH13,全片约70%-85%段落

**问题类型**: 倒计时压迫感缺失

**严重程度**: S级

**为什么不好**:

这是全片最致命的结构问题,直接背离标题与框架的核心承诺。

1. **主题承诺未兑现**: 论点卡明确说"崩溃是每一天都在发生",但CH10点名"820年"后,下一个时间锚点直接跳到CH13"822年2月"——中间18个月的"每一天"完全消失,变成了"崩溃是某一天发生的"。

2. **框架迁移失败**: 原片FS14"11:38 p.m. 2 minutes. I've been standing here for about 20 minutes"是**分钟级倒计时**,观众与主角一起盯着黑暗等待撞击。新版应该是**月度/年度倒计时**(820年3月,祭坛依然...820年雨季,石匠仍未...821年卡顿,只来了...822年2月,终于...),但现在直接跳过,失去戏剧反讽的核心张力。

3. **事实资源浪费**: F02明确列出五城时间线(帕伦克799→亚斯奇兰808→科潘822→蒂卡尔889→托尼那909),这是天然的"城市逐个熄灯"递进节奏,但只在CH10一笔带过"Palenque: 799. Yaxchilán: 808..."没有视觉化。

**问题来源**: 框架迁移问题+叙事节奏问题

**修改方向**:

在CH10与CH13之间**插入2-3个短段落**,每段30-50词,形成倒计时递进:

- **820年3月段**(FS11延伸): "三月过去。祭坛还是那个样子。我问过石匠工头——他说等雨季树长回来。"
- **820年雨季段**: "雨季到了。雨还是少。树没有长回来。广场上的人比上个月又少了。"
- **821年卡顿段**: "821年,卡顿周期仪式。往年会立新碑。今年没有。大祭司说明年。"
- **822年2月段**(现有CH13): "822年2月10日。Ukit Took登基。L祭坛还是那个样子。"

每段结尾用祭司的职业动作收束("我在历法轮上标记日期""我宣告下一个节庆""我走过那块祭坛"),强化"日常任务还在继续,但意义已经消失"的荒诞感。

**示范修改**:

```
[在CH10后插入]

820 AD, March. Three months since I asked about the altar. The carvers' foreman says they're waiting for the rainy season—waiting for trees to grow back.

I mark the date on my calendar wheel. Announce the next feast day. Forty people come.

Rainy season arrives. The rains—lighter than promised. The trees don't grow back. The carvers don't return.

821, the k'atun ceremony. Twenty years ago, we would have raised a new stela. This year, the high priest says: "Next k'atun."

I copy the date into the sacred calendar. Keep the wheels turning.

822 AD, February 10th. Ukit Took's coronation. That altar—still one face done, second started, two blank. The chisels right there.

[然后接回现有CH13]
```

## 五、整篇文案的深层问题检查

### 1. 主线问题

**核心问题是什么?**

明确:玛雅神王制的"永恒承诺"(国王放血→神降雨→文明延续)在崩溃期如何一项项失效,以及作为技术官僚的祭司如何目睹这个过程。

**是否围绕核心问题推进?**

基本是,但有两处偏离:
- CH03任务简报重复CH01内容,浪费篇幅
- CH09王宫奢侈段落过长,可压缩

**是否有更清晰的叙事方向?**

当前叙事是"空间探索(神庙→王宫)+时间倒计时(820→822)",双线并行。

更清晰的方向:**以L祭坛为主线锚点**,每个时间节点都回到祭坛("我又一次路过,凿子还在那里"),用重复结构强化"停滞"的荒诞感,目前这个锚点只在开头(CH01)和结尾(CH13-CH15)出现,中段消失。

### 2. 信息组织

**哪些是真正的新信息?**

- L祭坛雕到一半永久停工(F01)✓
- 灰泥地板越铺越薄=木材耗尽(F21)——**未使用**
- 五城时间线:帕伦克799→托尼那909(F02)——一笔带过,未视觉化
- 值年神仪式的五天禁忌(F07)——**未使用**
- 放血仪式的神学契约(F12)✓

**哪些在重复已有结论?**

- CH03"Two tasks"重复CH01 B6
- CH14"Attendance dropped...Hundreds used to come. Now fifty"数字重复表述

**缺少理解核心结论的必需信息?**

- **灰泥地板变薄**(F21):这是"木材耗尽"最直观的物证,比石匠的对话更有力,但完全未用
- **其他城市的消息**(F02五城时间线):如果祭司只看到科潘一城,他怎么知道"这不只是我们的问题"?需要补充商队/其他城市祭司带来的消息

**应该调整信息出现的顺序?**

- 灰泥地板变薄应在CH08王宫段落提前出现(祭司发现王宫新铺的地板比旧地板薄),这比CH09供品奢侈更直接证明"资源见底"

### 3. 留存机制

**开头是否建立了继续观看的理由?**

是。L祭坛+双任务线+真实性契约完成良好。

**中间是否持续提供新信息/冲突/认知变化?**

部分成立,但有两处平铺直叙:
- CH04-CH05日常职责段落(历法解释)过长,虽有现代参照系但缺少悬念
- CH08-CH09王宫段落缺乏冲突推进,只是奇观罗列

**是否只用转折词制造表面悬念?**

基本没有这个问题,文案较克制。

**观众是否能预料后续全部内容?**

FS11点名822年后,观众知道结局将至,但**不知道祭司会如何反应**——这是后段唯一悬念。目前FS13警告失败+FS15崩解独白处理合理,但FS14倒计时段落过短(见P01),削弱了"等待终点"的张力。

**结尾是否回答了前面提出的问题?**

是。开头问"为什么祭坛停工",结尾答"因为崩溃不是一天发生,而是每天的任务悄悄停止"。

### 4. 内容可靠性

**事实是否有依据?**

绝大部分有,但有三处需标注:
1. CH14"500→50人"(F33推测)未标注
2. CH12国王话术(F32假设)未标注
3. CH13"carvers didn't return"(F01祭坛停工有据,但"石匠为何不回来"是推论)

**推理是否成立?**

成立。从木材耗尽→灰泥减少→祭坛停工→人口流失的因果链有考古支撑(F18-F22)。

**是否把假设当成事实?**

CH14仪式观众数字有此风险,需补充标注。

**是否缺少关键限定条件?**

需补充:这是**南部低地**的崩溃,北方尤卡坦同期人口上升(F22)。目前只在事实表中有,正文未提及,可能让观众以为"整个玛雅文明灭绝"。

建议在结尾前增加一句(10-15词):"北方的城市还在。人们往那里走。但南方——我们这里——停了。"

### 5. 原创性与题材独立性

**新文案是否建立了自己的核心矛盾?**

是。**"维持永恒 vs 永恒停止"**是玛雅题材独有的,与泰坦尼克"豪华客轮 vs 冰山"完全不同。

**是否建立了自己的内容材料?**

是。科巴香、树皮纸、放血仪式、历法轮盘等考据细节均为玛雅专属。

**是否建立了自己的解释路径?**

基本是,但FS09王宫奇观段落与原片结构过于相似(材质对比→空间尺度→"same city/boat"句式),可适当调整表达。

**哪些部分需要重新设计?**

- CH10五城时间线需要视觉化/叙事化,不能只是年份罗列
- CH08-CH09王宫段落需要增加祭司的**选择困境**:他看到奢侈与匮乏并存,是继续执行仪式假装正常,还是现在就去警告国王?这个内心冲突目前缺失

| P1 | CH14 | 崩解段落缺乏空间化场景,只有抽象数字 | 增加祭司站在广场固定位置的空间对比(50-80词):"我站在第五级台阶...往年看不见对面墙,今年能数清每块石砖" | 情绪峰值必须有具体画面支撑,当前过于抽象 | 否,逻辑推论即可 |
| P1 | CH01 B6 | 开头信息过载,150词堆叠6个任务点 | 拆成两段,第一段只说探索目标,第二段说警告任务,删除"崩溃不是一天发生"的元评论 | 开头45秒决定留存率,当前过载削弱冲击力 | 否,删减即可 |
| P1 | CH11 | 调性切换未完成,仍保留日常轻快节奏 | 增加情绪前置段落(30-50词):"我不想这一天到来...想着广场上那些还在等雨的人",删除"pack incense"日常化动作 | FS11点名日期后必须归零,当前未做到 | 否,情绪描写即可 |
| P2 | CH08 | 禁区奇观情绪峰值不足,过于克制 | 强化祭司情绪反应,增加资源换算(玉石=十人抬一月)+愤怒质疑:"我想告诉他们,这不是永恒" | 探索线情感奖励不足 | 否,推论即可 |
| P2 | CH03 | 任务简报重复CH01内容 | 删除"Two tasks"句,直接进入日常职责描写 | 浪费篇幅削弱B6冲击 | 否,删减即可 |
| P2 | CH15 | 结尾缺少最后画面定格 | 补充祭司再次走过祭坛的具体画面:"凿子还在那里,两年的灰尘" | 结尾需要视觉化意象,不只是抽象评论 | 否,F01已足够 |
| P2 | CH12 | 国王话术不够神圣威严,像现代政客 | 缩短为20-30词宣告式短句,删除解释性语句 | 神王权威感不足削弱"无法说服"的合理性 | 否,改写即可 |
| P2 | CH04 | 阶层冲突缺乏具体事件 | 增加守卫让祭司等待+高级祭司径直通过的场景(40-60词) | 第一次让观众"感受"等级,当前过于抽象 | 否,逻辑推论即可 |
| P2 | CH09 | 缺少"阶层麻木"观察 | 补充贵族看到供品的无反应(30-40词):"没有一个人皱眉,这就是正常" | 繁荣顶点需要"麻木"制造不安感 | 否,推论即可 |
| P2 | CH14 | 仪式观众数字未标注推测性质 | 首次使用时增加标注:"我无法证明这个数字,但广场告诉你" | 维护真实性契约 | 否,标注即可 |
| P2 | CH07 | 关键配角未铺垫,突然出现 | CH06提前一句介绍"那位教过我历法的老祭司" | 配角存在感薄弱 | 否,补充即可 |
| P2 | CH05 | 感官细节层次单薄,只有视嗅觉 | 补充触觉/温度(树皮纸质感/石桌温度/跪坐腿麻)2-3处,每处10-15词 | 日常生活流需要多感官沉浸 | 否,推论即可 |
| P2 | 全篇 | 灰泥地板变薄(F21)这一关键物证完全未使用 | 在CH08王宫段落增加祭司发现地板变薄的观察(20-30词) | F21是"木材耗尽"最直观证据,比对话更有力 | 否,F21已给出 |

### 最值得先修改的三个地方

**1. P0-倒计时段落缺失(CH10-CH13)** 
**为什么先改**: 这是全片核心主题"崩溃是每天发生"的唯一支撑。当前820年直接跳到822年,观众只看到两个时间点,无法体验"缓慢倒计时"的压迫感,框架迁移核心失败。修复后,戏剧反讽张力从0分提升到7-8分,连带提升P1情绪崩解段落的说服力(因为观众已经跟着祭司"等待"了18个月)。

**2. P0-标题与内容不匹配**
**为什么先改**: 这是发布层面的问题。标题承诺"多城崩溃",内容聚焦"一城一坛",观众会觉得被误导。修改标题(改为单数)是零成本高收益的修复,立刻解决承诺-内容匹配问题,提升8分→10分。

**3. P1-归属感峰值缺失(CH06)**
**为什么先改**: CH06是情绪曲线的第一个峰值,也是后段崩解的情感燃料。当前只有仪式动作描写,观众无法与祭司或共同体建立情感连接,导致CH14"I can't watch this"的崩解失去支撑。补充40-60词主观感受,情绪递进从6分提升到8-9分。

### 连带影响

- **修复P0倒计时** → 自动修复P1调性切换问题(因为增加的时间节点段落本身就是沉重倒计时语气,冲淡了当前CH11-CH13的轻快感)
- **修复P1归属感峰值** → 提升P1崩解段落的情感说服力(观众已经爱上那个共同体,看到它消失才会心碎)
- **修复P2禁区奇观情绪** → 强化全片"批判神王制"的暗线(看到奢侈→愤怒→警告国王的动机更充分)

### 已经有效,不应随意改动的部分

1. **CH01开场L祭坛意象**:具象有力,全片最好的锚点
2. **CH01真实性契约(B4)**:声明清晰,建立信任
3. **CH05历法复杂度的现代参照系**:"比阴历复杂十倍"让观众秒懂
4. **CH10日期点名**:调性切换开关到位
5. **CH15主题对照句**:"读过vs活过"论点成立

这些部分已经成功迁移框架或形成独特价值,不要因为追求"不同"而改动。

---

## 七、三种修改路线及推荐方案

### A. 最小修改(保结构,修关键)

**适用情况**: 时间紧迫,只修复阻碍发布的核心问题

**主要修改范围**:
1. 修改标题(单数"City")
2. CH01 B6拆段,删减信息过载
3. CH10-CH13插入2个倒计时节点段落(820年雨季+821年卡顿)
4. CH14补充空间化场景(广场对比)
5. CH06补充归属感金句(40词)

**优势**: 
- 改动量最小(新增约150词,删减约50词)
- 保留现有95%内容
- 修复P0+部分P1问题,总分可提升至82-85分

**代价**: 
- P2细节问题未解决(感官层次/配角铺垫/阶层麻木等)
- 王宫段落(CH08-CH09)仍略显拖沓
- 灰泥地板(F21)等强力物证未使用

**对当前文案是否值得采用**: **值得**,如果目标是"尽快发布可用版本"。修复后可达到基本发布标准,但非最优状态。

---

### B. 结构优化(调顺序,补逻辑,删重复)

**适用情况**: 有时间进行一轮中等强度修改,追求更好留存效果

**主要修改范围**:
1. 执行A路线全部修改
2. 删除CH03任务简报重复段落
3. CH04增加阶层冲突具体事件(守卫/等待场景)
4. CH05补充感官细节(触觉/温度3处)
5. CH07提前铺垫资深祭司角色
6. CH08增加灰泥地板变薄的物证观察
7. CH08强化禁区奇观情绪峰值(资源换算+愤怒)
8. CH09补充阶层麻木观察
9. CH11增加情绪前置段落
10. CH12改写国王话术(神圣简洁化)
11. CH14标注数字推测性质
12. CH15补充最后画面定格

**优势**:
- 解决P0+P1+大部分P2问题
- 总分可提升至88-92分
- 留存机制显著优化(情绪峰值+倒计时+细节密度全面提升)
- 考据感增强(灰泥地板+感官细节)

**代价**:
- 改动量中等(新增约400词,删减约100词,改写约200词)
- 需要重新调整6-8个章节
- 耗时约为A路线的3倍

**对当前文案是否值得采用**: **强烈推荐**。这是性价比最高的方案,修改量可控且效果显著,可达到"优秀可发布"标准。

---

### C. 深度重构(重建主线,强化意象)

**适用情况**: 追求爆款品质,愿意投入大量时间重写

**主要修改范围**:
1. 执行B路线全部修改
2. **重建倒计时主线**:不只是插入时间节点,而是让祭司在每个节点都回到L祭坛("我又一次路过,凿子还在那里"),用**重复结构**强化"停滞"的荒诞感(目前祭坛只在开头和结尾出现,中段消失)
3. **增加五城时间线叙事化**:不只是年份罗列,而是让祭司听到其他城市的消息——"商队从帕伦克来,说那里23年没立新碑了""亚斯奇兰的祭司说他们城里只剩..."——让"城市逐个熄灯"视觉化(如果保留复数标题)
4. **重构王宫段落(CH08-CH09)**:压缩奇观罗列,增加**祭司的内心冲突**——看到奢侈与匮乏并存,他在"继续执行仪式假装正常 vs 现在就去警告"之间挣扎(这是当前缺失的核心两难)
5. **强化配角命运暗示**:CH05助手说"儿子学文字"后,CH14倒计时段落点一句"我再也没见过那个助手",或结尾段落"我不知道他们去了哪里"——让人化的配角成为具体损失
6. **补充北方迁移信息**(F22):结尾前一句"北方的城市还在,人们往那里走,但南方——我们这里——停了",避免观众误以为整个玛雅灭绝

**优势**:
- 解决全部P0+P1+P2问题
- 总分可达95-98分
- 主题意象(L祭坛)贯穿全片,结构完整性最高
- 情感重量最足(配角命运+内心冲突+重复结构)
- 如果保留复数标题,五城时间线叙事化可完全兑现标题承诺

**代价**:
- 改动量大(新增约800词,删减约200词,改写约500词)
- 需要重构3-4个章节的叙事逻辑
- 耗时约为B路线的2-3倍
- 存在过度修改风险(如果控制不好,可能失去当前文案的简洁克制)

**对当前文案是否值得采用**: **如果追求爆款品质,值得**。但需要评估时间成本与收益——从88分提升到96分的边际收益,是否值得3倍的时间投入?如果这是系列内容的首篇(需要立标杆),值得;如果只是常规选题,B路线已足够。

---

## 八、最终推荐方案

**推荐路线: B(结构优化)**

**理由**:

1. **性价比最优**: 当前文案已有良好基础(76分),B路线修改量可控(约3-4小时工作量)但效果显著(提升至88-92分),可达到"优秀可发布"标准。

2. **核心问题全覆盖**: P0两个致命问题(倒计时缺失+标题不匹配)全部修复,P1影响留存的关键问题(归属感+崩解场景+开头过载+调性切换)全部解决,P2大部分细节优化到位。

3. **避免过度修改风险**: 当前文案的简洁克制是优点(无冗余解释/无煽情堆砌),C路线虽能冲击更高分,但存在"改过头"风险,可能失去当前的节制美感。B路线在优化与保留之间平衡最好。

4. **时间-收益比合理**: 从76分到88分的提升,对观众留存率的影响远大于从88分到96分。根据YouTube算法,内容质量过"基本线"(约85分)后,标题/缩略图/前30秒的优化重要性反而上升——与其花3倍时间冲击96分,不如用B路线快速达到88分,然后把时间投入到标题测试与开头A/B测试。

5. **框架迁移已基本成功**: 双任务线+调性切换+戏剧反讽的核心机制已经成立,只是部分阶段功能未充分实现(归属感/奇观情绪/倒计时密度)。B路线补足这些"未完成"即可,无需推倒重来。

**不推荐C路线的原因**: 
C路线的重复结构("每个节点都回到祭坛")与五城时间线叙事化,虽然理论上更完美,但可能让中段节奏过于缓慢(观众已经知道祭坛停工了,反复回去看可能产生疲劳)。除非这是系列首篇需要立标杆,否则B路线已经足够好。

**不推荐A路线的原因**: 
A路线虽快,但P2细节问题(感官层次/阶层麻木/情绪峰值)积累起来会让文案停留在"合格"而非"优秀"。多投入50%的时间(B相比A),换来的留存率提升(88分vs82分)是值得的。

---

issues.problem: 820-822年中间18个月消失,直接跳到终点,失去"缓慢崩溃"核心主题
issues.direction: 插入2-3个月度/年度时间节点段落,形成递进倒计时
issues.detail:
### 问题编号:P01

**原文位置**: CH10-CH13,全片约70%-85%段落

**问题类型**: 倒计时压迫感缺失

**严重程度**: S级

**为什么不好**:

这是全片最致命的结构问题,直接背离标题与框架的核心承诺。

1. **主题承诺未兑现**: 论点卡明确说"崩溃是每一天都在发生",但CH10点名"820年"后,下一个时间锚点直接跳到CH13"822年2月"——中间18个月的"每一天"完全消失,变成了"崩溃是某一天发生的"。

2. **框架迁移失败**: 原片FS14"11:38 p.m. 2 minutes. I've been standing here for about 20 minutes"是**分钟级倒计时**,观众与主角一起盯着黑暗等待撞击。新版应该是**月度/年度倒计时**(820年3月,祭坛依然...820年雨季,石匠仍未...821年卡顿,只来了...822年2月,终于...),但现在直接跳过,失去戏剧反讽的核心张力。

3. **事实资源浪费**: F02明确列出五城时间线(帕伦克799→亚斯奇兰808→科潘822→蒂卡尔889→托尼那909),这是天然的"城市逐个熄灯"递进节奏,但只在CH10一笔带过"Palenque: 799. Yaxchilán: 808..."没有视觉化。

**问题来源**: 框架迁移问题+叙事节奏问题

**修改方向**:

在CH10与CH13之间**插入2-3个短段落**,每段30-50词,形成倒计时递进:

- **820年3月段**(FS11延伸): "三月过去。祭坛还是那个样子。我问过石匠工头——他说等雨季树长回来。"
- **820年雨季段**: "雨季到了。雨还是少。树没有长回来。广场上的人比上个月又少了。"
- **821年卡顿段**: "821年,卡顿周期仪式。往年会立新碑。今年没有。大祭司说明年。"
- **822年2月段**(现有CH13): "822年2月10日。Ukit Took登基。L祭坛还是那个样子。"

每段结尾用祭司的职业动作收束("我在历法轮上标记日期""我宣告下一个节庆""我走过那块祭坛"),强化"日常任务还在继续,但意义已经消失"的荒诞感。

**示范修改**:

```
[在CH10后插入]

820 AD, March. Three months since I asked about the altar. The carvers' foreman says they're waiting for the rainy season—waiting for trees to grow back.

I mark the date on my calendar wheel. Announce the next feast day. Forty people come.

Rainy season arrives. The rains—lighter than promised. The trees don't grow back. The carvers don't return.

821, the k'atun ceremony. Twenty years ago, we would have raised a new stela. This year, the high priest says: "Next k'atun."

I copy the date into the sacred calendar. Keep the wheels turning.

822 AD, February 10th. Ukit Took's coronation. That altar—still one face done, second started, two blank. The chisels right there.

[然后接回现有CH13]
```

---

issues.problem: 仪式段落只有动作描写,缺少"我是我们中一员"的主观情感体验
issues.direction: 增加祭司在仪式中的归属感金句(40-60词)
issues.detail:
### 问题编号:P02

**原文位置**: CH06,全篇约35%处

**问题类型**: 归属感峰值未实现

**严重程度**: A级

**为什么不好**:

FS07在框架中的功能是"情绪高峰,为后段失去蓄能"——原片舞会段落的核心不是舞蹈本身,而是"I don't know what I'm doing, but nobody seems to care, and I think that's the whole point"这句归属感金句。观众需要先爱上这个共同体,后段崩解才有情感重量。

现有CH06写了仪式的视觉元素(火把/鼓/血),但**缺少祭司的主观情感体验**:
- "This is our promise. We bleed, they send rain"只是神学机制说明,非情感共鸣
- "The whole plaza believes it. Certainty. Shared commitment"是旁观者总结,非参与者感受

观众无法通过这段与祭司或仪式群体建立情感连接,后面FS15"I can't watch this"的崩解就失去支撑。

**问题来源**: 框架迁移问题(误把场景描写当情绪峰值)

**修改方向**:

在CH06仪式描写后,**增加祭司的主观感受段落**(40-60词),捕捉"个体融入集体"的瞬间:

重点不是仪式多壮观,而是"我作为一个会算错日期、担心祭坛停工的焦虑个体,在这一刻被集体仪式的确定性治愈"。

**示范修改**:

```
[在现有CH06"Shared commitment."后插入]

When my blood hits the bark paper, I forget about the empty altar. The chisels waiting. The carvers who didn't return.

In this firelight, every face looks the same. Noble, commoner, priest—we're all bleeding the same promise.

For this one night, I'm not the priest who notices the crowd shrinking. I'm just one of us. And the gods—they have to be listening.

[然后接"That night, ceremony ends..."继续现有剧情]
```

issues.problem: B6价值承诺150词堆叠6个任务点,削弱冲击力
issues.direction: 拆成两段,删除元评论,先探索后警告
issues.detail:
### 问题编号:P03

**原文位置**: CH01 B6(FS01末尾),第45秒附近

**问题类型**: 开头信息过载

**严重程度**: A级

**为什么不好**:

B6价值承诺段现有150词,在45秒内堆叠了6个任务点:
1. 进王宫礼仪区
2. 看国王放血仪式
3. 看精英卡顿仪式
4. 找国王/大祭司
5. 告诉他们(木材耗尽+观众减少+雨未至)
6. 解释崩溃不是一天发生

违反"开头锁定"规则中"不要加报流程的议程句",且在观众尚未建立任何情感投入时塞入过多承诺,削弱每个承诺的冲击力。

原片B6是58词,只说两件事:探索(first class, dining rooms, grand staircase)+警告(talk to the captain about the iceberg),简洁有力。

**问题来源**: 开头吸引力问题+框架迁移过度

**修改方向**:

将B6拆成两段,第一段只说探索目标(王宫+仪式),第二段说警告任务,用"But there's something else"/"And I need to do something"过渡。删除"崩溃不是一天发生"的元评论(这是结尾论点,不该在开头剧透)。

**示范修改**:

```
[替换现有B6]

Here's what I'm going to do. I want to see the royal palace zones I don't normally enter—the king's bloodletting altar, the elite katun rituals, all of it.

And I need to find the king or the high priest. Tell them what I'm seeing. The stone carvers say we've run out of trees. Ritual attendance is dropping. The rains the king promised—they haven't come.

I don't know if they'll listen. But someone has to say it.
```
(92词,删减38%,保留核心承诺)
